00 · Start Here

This is a self-contained course, not a reference manual. It is written for someone who wants to become a network engineer and has no idea where to start.

What this book is

  • A curriculum, ordered so that nothing depends on a concept you have not seen yet.
  • A field guide. Every chapter ends with "what breaks" and "how to prove it".
  • Vendor-neutral first. Cisco syntax appears as an example, but the ideas are the same on Juniper, Arista, FRR, or a Linux box.

What this book is not

  • Not a certification dump. Certifications come after understanding, not instead of it.
  • Not a list of commands. Commands change; the model in your head does not.

How to read it

Use three passes per chapter. Do not skip the third one — it is where learning happens.

Pass What you do Time
1. Read Read the chapter once, without stopping to memorise 20 min
2. Draw Close the book and draw the diagram or the flow from memory 10 min
3. Explain Explain it out loud, as if to a friend who knows nothing 10 min

If step 3 is hard, you did not understand it yet. Re-read only the part that failed.

The five questions to ask about any technology

  1. What problem does it solve? (If you cannot answer, it is trivia.)
  2. What does it look like on the wire? (Bytes, headers, ports.)
  3. What does it look like in the config? (Where do I turn it on?)
  4. What does it look like when it breaks? (Symptom -> cause.)
  5. How do I prove it works? (Which command, which capture.)

Every chapter in this book answers all five.

What you need

  • A computer with a browser and a terminal.
  • Network Lab, the browser-based simulator linked in the page toolbar, for hands-on practice with Labs 01, 02 and 04.
  • WSL2 + containerlab + netlab for real routing labs with FRR.
  • Wireshark, free.
  • A notebook. Physical is better. Draw topologies by hand.

The honest timeline

Level What you can do Realistic time
Beginner Explain OSI, subnet a /24, build a small LAN 4 weeks
Junior Configure VLANs, OSPF, static routes, ACLs, NAT 3 months
Intermediate Design a small network, run BGP, troubleshoot with captures 9 months
Employable Own a network, automate it, explain your decisions 12–18 months

Anyone who promises two weeks is selling something.

The rule that matters most

A network engineer is not someone who memorised commands. It is someone who can predict what the packets will do, and prove it.

That is the whole job. Everything in this book serves that sentence.

01 · What Networking Really Is

Strip away the marketing and a network is three things: hosts, links, and rules.

The smallest possible network

Two computers and one cable.

[ PC-A ]====================[ PC-B ]
  192.168.1.10              192.168.1.20

For A to send a file to B, four things must be true:

  1. A must know B's address (IP address).
  2. A must know how to reach it (same subnet -> send directly; different -> send to a router).
  3. A must know B's hardware address (MAC address, found with ARP).
  4. Both must agree on the rules (Ethernet framing, IP, TCP or UDP, ports).

Everything else in networking is a variation of these four problems at a larger scale.

Why layers exist

Imagine writing one program that handles: the electrical signal, the cable type, the addressing scheme, retransmission, encryption, and the file format. Now imagine changing Wi-Fi and having to rewrite the file format code.

Layers let each part change independently. Wi-Fi replaces Ethernet without changing TCP. IPv6 replaces IPv4 without changing HTTP. This is the single most important idea in networking.

The cast of characters

Term Meaning Example
Host / endpoint A device with an IP that sends or receives laptop, server, phone, router interface
Link The physical or logical connection between two devices copper cable, fiber, Wi-Fi, a tunnel
Node Any device on the network switch, router, firewall, host
Packet A unit of data with headers an IP packet
Frame A packet wrapped in a Layer-2 header an Ethernet frame
Segment A TCP/UDP unit TCP segment
Protocol An agreed set of rules TCP, OSPF, DNS

LAN, WAN, and the Internet

  • LAN (Local Area Network) — one administrative domain, usually one building or floor. High speed, low latency, you control it.
  • WAN (Wide Area Network) — connects sites over a provider's infrastructure. Lower speed relative to cost, higher latency, you do not control the middle.
  • The Internet — the WAN of WANs. A network of networks that agree to exchange routes using BGP.

A network engineer usually owns the LAN edge, the WAN edge, and the policy between them.

Circuit switching vs packet switching

Old telephone networks reserved a path for the whole call. If you were not talking, the capacity was still reserved and wasted.

The Internet does not reserve anything. It chops data into packets and lets each packet find its own way. This is why:

  • links can be shared by thousands of users
  • a failed link can be routed around
  • but quality is not guaranteed — hence QoS, buffers, and congestion

Bandwidth, latency, throughput, jitter

These four get confused constantly. Learn the difference now.

Term Meaning Analogy
Bandwidth Maximum capacity of a link Width of a highway
Latency Time for one bit to travel How long one car takes
Throughput Actual data delivered per second Cars that arrive per hour
Jitter Variation in latency Uneven traffic flow

A 1 Gbps link with 200 ms latency still feels slow for interactive work. A 100 Mbps link with 2 ms latency feels instant. Latency is usually the real problem.

The bandwidth-delay product

The amount of data "in flight" on a path:

BDP = bandwidth × round-trip time

On a 1 Gbps link with 100 ms RTT, 100 million bits (about 12.5 MB) can be in flight. If the TCP window is smaller than that, you will never fill the link. This is why long, fast paths need window scaling — and why "the link is 1 Gbps but the file transfer is slow" is a real and common problem.

What a network engineer actually does

Activity Share of the job
Designing and documenting 20%
Configuring and changing 25%
Troubleshooting 35%
Automating and improving 20%

Troubleshooting is the biggest slice. That is why this book keeps returning to "what does it look like when it breaks".

02 · The Models: OSI and TCP/IP

The OSI model is not a protocol. It is a mental checklist that lets you say "this is a Layer 2 problem" and stop guessing.

The two models side by side

   OSI (7 layers)                 TCP/IP (4 layers)
   ------------------             ---------------------
 7 Application  ┐
 6 Presentation ├──────────────►  Application  (HTTP, DNS, SSH, TLS)
 5 Session      ┘
 4 Transport    ──────────────►  Transport    (TCP, UDP, QUIC)
 3 Network      ──────────────►  Internet     (IP, ICMP, OSPF, BGP)
 2 Data Link    ┐
 1 Physical     ┴─────────────►  Link         (Ethernet, Wi-Fi, ARP)

The industry still speaks OSI ("Layer 2 switch", "Layer 3 problem", "Layer 7 firewall"). TCP/IP is what actually runs. Learn OSI to communicate, TCP/IP to build.

What each layer does, and what breaks there

Layer Job Units Typical failure First thing to check
7 Application User-facing protocol Data wrong URL, certificate, app config can you curl it from the host?
6 Presentation Encoding, encryption Data TLS version, cipher mismatch TLS handshake in Wireshark
5 Session Conversation state Data idle timeout, auth session drop logs, timeout settings
4 Transport End-to-end delivery, ports Segment/Datagram firewall blocking port, retransmits ss -tulpn, capture
3 Network Addressing, routing Packet wrong route, ACL, asymmetric path ping, traceroute, routing table
2 Data Link Local delivery, MAC Frame VLAN mismatch, STP loop, duplex switch MAC table, error counters
1 Physical Bits on the medium Bits bad cable, dirty fiber, no light link lights, ethtool, cable test

Rule of thumb: 80% of "network problems" are Layer 1, 2, or a DNS mistake.

Encapsulation

Data moves down the stack on the sender, and up on the receiver.

Sender                              Receiver
HTTP request                        "GET /index.html"
  │                                 ▲
  ▼                                 │
TCP header + data    [TCP|DATA]     │
  │                                 │
  ▼                                 │
IP header            [IP|TCP|DATA]  │
  │                                 │
  ▼                                 │
Ethernet header      [ETH|IP|TCP|DATA|FCS]
  │                                 │
  └──────── wire ───────────────────┘

Each layer adds its own header. At the receiving side, each layer strips its header and hands the payload up. This is why you can capture a single frame and read the entire stack inside it.

MTU and fragmentation

  • MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) — the largest payload a link can carry. Ethernet default: 1500 bytes.
  • If an IP packet is bigger than the MTU and DF (don't fragment) is set, the router sends back ICMP "fragmentation needed".
  • If DF is not set, the packet is fragmented. Fragmentation is expensive and often breaks firewalls.

Common MTU problems:

Symptom Cause
Ping works, large transfers hang path MTU black hole, ICMP blocked
VPN works for small packets only tunnel overhead reduced MTU, no MSS clamping
SSH connects then freezes MTU/MSS issue on the path

MTU by technology: Ethernet 1500, VLAN tag −4, GRE −24, IPsec −50 to −73, VXLAN −50.

Ports: how one IP carries many conversations

A connection is identified by the 5-tuple:

source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, protocol

That is how your laptop holds 200 connections to the same server on port 443 and keeps them all separate.

Range Name Notes
0–1023 Well-known HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, SSH 22, DNS 53
1024–49151 Registered vendor-specific services
49152–65535 Ephemeral client-side source ports

See Appendix A for the full port table you actually need.

The troubleshooting ladder

When something is broken, walk the stack. Do not skip.

  1. L1: Is the link up? ip link, ethtool eth0, LED, show interface
  2. L2: Is the MAC reachable? ip neigh, show mac address-table, VLAN correct?
  3. L3: Is there a route? ip route, show ip route, ping, traceroute
  4. L4: Is the port open? ss -tulpn, nc -vz host port, firewall rules
  5. L7: Does the app answer? curl -v, dig, logs

Each step answers a yes/no question. Once a step fails, stop and fix that — do not "try random things" at Layer 7 when the cable is unplugged.

03 · Ethernet, MAC Addresses, and Switching

Ethernet is Layer 2. It moves frames between devices on the same local network. It does not know about IP, and it does not route.

The Ethernet frame

+---------+---------+---------+----------+-------------+-----+
| Dst MAC | Src MAC |  Type   | Payload  |     FCS     | IFG |
| 6 bytes | 6 bytes | 2 bytes | 46-1500  |   4 bytes   |     |
+---------+---------+---------+----------+-------------+-----+
Field Purpose
Destination MAC Who should receive this frame
Source MAC Who sent it
Type What is inside: 0x0800 = IPv4, 0x86DD = IPv6, 0x8100 = VLAN tag, 0x0806 = ARP
Payload The IP packet
FCS CRC for error detection

Minimum frame: 64 bytes. Maximum: 1518 bytes (1522 with a VLAN tag). Frames outside that range are usually dropped as "runts" or "giants".

MAC addresses

A 48-bit address, written as six hex pairs: 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E.

  • First 3 bytes = OUI (manufacturer).
  • Last 3 bytes = assigned by the manufacturer.
  • Unicast — destined for one NIC.
  • Broadcast — FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF, every device in the broadcast domain.
  • Multicast — starts with 01:00:5E (IPv4) or 33:33 (IPv6) at the Ethernet level.

MAC addresses are local to the link. They are not routed. When a router forwards a packet to a new network, it writes new source and destination MACs for the next hop.

How a switch works

A switch is a Layer-2 device that learns which MAC lives on which port.

  1. Frame arrives on port 3 from AA:AA:...
  2. Switch records AA:AA -> port 3 in its MAC address table (CAM table).
  3. It looks up the destination MAC:
    • known -> forward out that port only (unicast)
    • unknown -> flood out all ports except the source (unknown unicast flood)
    • broadcast/multicast -> flood
  4. Frames age out of the table after ~300 seconds by default.
Cisco:  show mac address-table
Linux:  bridge fdb show

Collision domains and broadcast domains

  • A collision domain is a set of devices that can collide. Each switch port is its own collision domain. A hub is one big collision domain (avoid hubs).
  • A broadcast domain is a set of devices that receive each other's broadcasts. A switch (without VLANs) is one broadcast domain. A VLAN is a broadcast domain.

This distinction is the reason VLANs exist.

Duplex and speed

Mode Behaviour Symptom when mismatched
Full duplex send and receive at the same time —
Half duplex one direction at a time, uses CSMA/CD collisions, late collisions, slow throughput

Autonegotiation usually works. When it does not — often with old gear, or a hard-coded side — you get a duplex mismatch. Symptom: link is up, ping works, throughput is terrible, FCS/CRC and late-collision counters climb.

Cisco:  show interfaces | include duplex|collision|CRC
Linux:  ethtool eth0

ARP: finding a MAC from an IP

Before A can send a frame to B on the same subnet, it needs B's MAC.

A: "Who has 192.168.1.20? Tell 192.168.1.10"   -> broadcast FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF
B: "192.168.1.20 is at BB:BB:BB:BB:BB:BB"      -> unicast back to A

Then A caches the mapping. If the destination is on another subnet, A ARPs for the default gateway, not for the remote host — a detail that trips up a lot of beginners.

Cisco:  show arp
Linux:  ip neigh

Gratuitous ARP — an unsolicited ARP announcement, used when an interface comes up or an IP moves (failover). It is also the basis of ARP spoofing attacks.

Common Layer-2 attacks (and why they matter to you)

Attack How Defence
MAC flooding fill the CAM table so the switch floods everything port security, MAC limits
ARP spoofing answer ARP for the gateway Dynamic ARP Inspection, static entries
VLAN hopping double-tagged frames or trunk negotiation disable DTP, set access ports explicitly, native VLAN ≠ 1
STP takeover become the root bridge BPDU guard, root guard
DHCP starvation exhaust the DHCP pool DHCP snooping, port security

You do not need to be a security engineer, but you must know these exist because they are configured on switches you will touch.

Media types you will meet

Medium Distance Notes
Cat5e 100 m 1 Gbps
Cat6 / 6a 100 m 1 Gbps / 10 Gbps
Multimode fiber (OM3/OM4) 300–550 m 10–100 Gbps, cheap optics
Single-mode fiber kilometres long haul, expensive optics
DAC cable 1–5 m direct attach copper in racks
Wi-Fi varies shared medium, half duplex

Rule: copper inside the rack and to the desk, fiber between buildings and to the core.

04 · IP Addressing and Subnetting

This is the chapter people fear. It is just binary arithmetic with a shortcut.

The IPv4 address

32 bits, written as four decimal numbers: 192.168.10.25.

192      .168      .10       .25
11000000 .10101000 .00001010 .00011001

An address is split into a network part and a host part by the subnet mask.

IP:    192.168.10.25
Mask:  255.255.255.0    -> /24
       11111111.11111111.11111111.00000000
       |------ network ------|  hosts  |

The first N bits identify the network. The remaining bits identify the host.

CIDR and the block-size trick

Stop converting to binary for every subnet. Use this instead:

Block size = 256 − (mask octet)
Prefix Mask Block size Networks per /24 Usable hosts
/24 255.255.255.0 256 1 254
/25 255.255.255.128 128 2 126
/26 255.255.255.192 64 4 62
/27 255.255.255.224 32 8 30
/28 255.255.255.240 16 16 14
/29 255.255.255.248 8 32 6
/30 255.255.255.252 4 64 2
/31 255.255.255.254 2 128 2 (point-to-point)
/32 255.255.255.255 1 256 1 (host route)

Usable hosts = 2^(host bits) − 2 (network and broadcast are reserved).

Worked example: subnet 192.168.10.0/26

  • Block size: 256 − 192 = 64
  • Networks: .0, .64, .128, .192
  • For .64: network .64, broadcast .127, usable .65–.126
  • Hosts: 2^6 − 2 = 62

So 192.168.10.90 is in the .64 network. One step, no binary.

Second example: 10.1.1.200/27

  • Block size 32, networks: .0 .32 .64 .96 .128 .160 .192 .224
  • .200 falls in .192 → network 10.1.1.192, broadcast 10.1.1.223, usable .193–.222

VLSM: different sizes per subnet

Variable Length Subnet Masking = allocate from largest to smallest need.

Requirement: 100 hosts, 50 hosts, 25 hosts, and two point-to-point links, from 172.16.0.0/24.

Need Prefix Size Allocated
100 hosts /25 128 172.16.0.0/25
50 hosts /26 64 172.16.0.128/26
25 hosts /27 32 172.16.0.192/27
P2P /30 4 172.16.0.224/30
P2P /30 4 172.16.0.228/30
spare — — 172.16.0.232–255

Always allocate largest first. If you start with the /30s you will fragment the space.

Route summarization

A summary is the smallest prefix covering several networks. Convert to binary and take the common leading bits.

172.16.0.0/24   = 10101100.00010000.00000000
172.16.1.0/24   = 10101100.00010000.00000001
172.16.2.0/24   = 10101100.00010000.00000010
172.16.3.0/24   = 10101100.00010000.00000011
                  common: 22 bits      -> 172.16.0.0/22

Summaries reduce routing table size and make the network stable — if a /24 flaps, the summary does not.

Public, private, and special addresses

Range Name Notes
10.0.0.0/8 Private large enterprises
172.16.0.0/12 Private 172.16.0.0 – 172.31.255.255
192.168.0.0/16 Private home and small office
127.0.0.0/8 Loopback 127.0.0.1 = localhost
169.254.0.0/16 Link-local (APIPA) means DHCP failed
0.0.0.0/0 Default route "everything else"
224.0.0.0/4 Multicast OSPF 224.0.0.5, VRRP 224.0.0.18
240.0.0.0/4 Reserved —

169.254.x.x is a diagnostic gift: if a host has it, DHCP did not answer. Say that out loud in an interview and people notice.

Common traps

Trap Reality
"The gateway must be .1" Convention only. Any usable address works.
"A /24 always has 254 hosts" Only if the mask is /24. Check the mask.
Network and broadcast are usable No, except /31 (RFC 3021) and /32.
Overlapping subnets are fine They cause asymmetric routing and NAT chaos. Never overlap.
Renumbering is easy It is the most painful change in networking. Plan space up front.

Where each value is used

The same subnet has four look-alike values that do different jobs. Using the wrong one is a common configuration mistake.

Value Example in 10.0.0.16/28 Used for
Network address 10.0.0.16 Naming the subnet. Never assigned to a device.
Usable host IP .17 to .30 Interfaces, PCs, gateways.
Broadcast address .31 Last address. Never assigned.
Subnet mask 255.255.255.240 Interfaces, static routes, DHCP pools.
Wildcard mask 0.0.0.15 OSPF network, ACL matching (the inverse of the mask).
Task Example Value used
Router interface ip address 10.0.0.17 255.255.255.240 usable host IP + mask
Static route ip route 10.0.0.16 255.255.255.240 10.0.0.1 destination network + mask
OSPF network 10.0.0.16 0.0.0.15 area 0 network + wildcard
DHCP pool network 10.0.0.16 255.255.255.240 network + mask
ACL permit ip 10.0.0.16 0.0.0.15 any network + wildcard

How to practise

Do 10 problems a day for two weeks. Write the network, broadcast, and usable range for random addresses. Use ipcalc to check yourself:

ipcalc 192.168.10.90/26

Speed comes from repetition, not from reading.

04B · IPv4 & IPv6 Calculator

Everything in this chapter runs in your browser. Type an address, change the prefix, and every field updates. There are six tabs: IPv4, IPv6, VLSM, IPv6 Split, Practice, and Reference.

The point is not to skip the arithmetic. The point is to see it happen: every result comes with the bits that produced it, so a wrong hand calculation is easy to trace back to the exact bit you got wrong.

What the calculator gives you

IPv4 IPv6
Binary of the address and the mask 8 hextets with hex, decimal, and 16-bit binary
Network address (the AND operation) Expanded and RFC 5952 compressed form
Broadcast address Network prefix and last address
First and last usable host Address count in the prefix
Usable host count Address type (global, link-local, ULA, multicast, …)
Subnet mask and wildcard mask Interface ID
Block size and the interesting octet 128-bit binary view
Class, private/public, special ranges SLAAC and planning guidance
IPv4-mapped IPv6 forms —

Beyond the two columns above, the calculator also has a VLSM planner, an IPv6 splitter, a MAC → EUI-64 helper, and a prefix overlap checker.

Worked example: 15.168.1.1/17

Follow the five steps.

Step 1 — mask. /17 means 17 network bits.

11111111.11111111.10000000.00000000
   255  .   255  .   128  .    0

Step 2 — block size. The interesting octet is the third one (192 → 128 → block 256 − 128 = 128).

Step 3 — network. The third octet is 1. The multiples of 128 are 0 and 128. The highest one at or below 1 is 0.

15.168.1.1  AND  255.255.128.0  =  15.168.0.0

Step 4 — broadcast. Next block starts at 15.168.128.0, so broadcast is 15.168.127.255.

Step 5 — usable range and hosts.

first host  15.168.0.1
last host   15.168.127.254
hosts       2^(32−17) − 2 = 32768 − 2 = 32766

Check those numbers against the calculator below. They should match exactly.

Worked example: an IPv6 address at /48

Take 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334/48.

Step 1 — split into 8 hextets.

2001 : 0db8 : 85a3 : 0000 : 0000 : 8a2e : 0370 : 7334

Step 2 — /48 keeps the first three hextets. Everything after is the interface ID.

network = 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000

Step 3 — last address in the prefix is the network with all host bits set to 1.

2001:0db8:85a3:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff

Step 4 — compress. Drop leading zeros, then replace the longest run of zero groups with :: once.

2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334   ->   2001:db8:85a3::8a2e:370:7334

Step 5 — count. 128 − 48 = 80 host bits, so 2^80 addresses — about 1.2 × 10^24.

VLSM in five steps

VLSM means variable length subnet mask: inside the same address block, different subnets can have different sizes. A /24 for four departments does not have to be four /26s.

Example: 10.0.0.0/24, with Sales 50 hosts, IT 20, Voice 10, and one point-to-point link.

Step 1 — sort the requirements biggest first. 50, 20, 10, 2.

Step 2 — size each subnet. Find the smallest host bits n where 2^n − 2 ≥ hosts.

Requirement Host bits Usable Prefix
50 6 62 /26
20 5 30 /27
10 4 14 /28
2 2 2 /30

Step 3 — place each block at the next aligned address.

Sales   10.0.0.0/26     .0    - .63
IT      10.0.0.64/27    .64   - .95
Voice   10.0.0.96/28    .96   - .111
P2P     10.0.0.112/30   .112  - .115

Step 4 — see what is left. .116 to .255 = 140 addresses still free.

Step 5 — check alignment. Every block starts on a multiple of its own size. /26 starts at 0, /27 at 64, /28 at 96, /30 at 112. If a block does not start on a multiple of its size, the plan is wrong.

That is exactly what the VLSM tab does — put the base and the host counts in, and it returns the table above. If the requirements do not fit, it tells you which one failed.

Splitting a /48 into /64s

A /48 has 16 subnet bits left before the interface ID, so it contains 2^16 = 65,536 /64s.

2001:db8:1234:0000::/64
2001:db8:1234:0001::/64
2001:db8:1234:0002::/64
...
2001:db8:1234:ffff::/64

Only the fourth hextet changes. The first three hextets are the site prefix, and the last four are the interface ID.

Allocation Contains
/32 to an ISP 65,536 /48 sites
/48 to a site 65,536 /64 LANs
/56 to a home 256 /64 LANs
/64 to one LAN 18.4 quintillion addresses

Do not subnet a /64 further. SLAAC needs the host part to stay 64 bits, and every device on the LAN expects the same prefix length.

The other two tools

MAC → EUI-64. Flip the universal/local bit of the first octet (XOR the second-least significant bit of the first byte), then insert ff:fe in the middle.

00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e
 ^^ flip bit 1 of 0x00 -> 0x02
02:1a:2b  ff:fe  3c:4d:5e      interface ID
fe80::21a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e/64    link-local address

Overlap checker. Two prefixes either share no address at all, are identical, or one is inside the other. If two prefixes share addresses but neither contains the other, one of them is misaligned — that is a configuration error.

The calculator

IPv4 address
. . .
Prefix
/

The AND operation

The network address is the IP address AND the subnet mask, bit by bit. 1 AND 1 = 1. Everything else = 0.

What each bit is worth

The 30-second method
  1. Block size = 256 − the mask octet in the interesting octet (e.g. 192 → 64).
  2. Network = the highest multiple of the block size that is ≤ your address.
  3. Broadcast = the next block start − 1.
  4. Usable = network + 1 through broadcast − 1.
  5. Hosts = 2(32 − prefix) − 2.
IPv6 address
Prefix
/

Hextet breakdown

Each of the 8 groups is 16 bits. Hex digit → 4 bits. Two bytes per group.

128 bits

IPv6 compression rules (RFC 5952)
  1. Drop leading zeros in each group: 0db8 → db8.
  2. Replace one run of two or more all-zero groups with ::.
  3. If there is a tie, compress the first run.
  4. Never use :: more than once in an address.
  5. Never shorten a single zero group — write 0, not ::.
IPv6 planning rules
  • /32 to an ISP, /48 to a site, /56 to a home or small branch.
  • /64 for every LAN — SLAAC requires the host part to be 64 bits.
  • /128 for a single interface (loopback, host route).
  • /127 for point-to-point links (RFC 6164) — avoids the all-zeros subnet-router anycast address.

MAC address to EUI-64 (SLAAC)

Flip the universal/local bit of the first octet, then insert ff:fe in the middle. That is the interface ID a router gives you in a Router Advertisement.

MAC address
Base network (CIDR)
 
 

Enter how many hosts each subnet needs. They are allocated biggest-first, so the large blocks are not blocked by a small one.

How VLSM works
  1. Sort the requirements from biggest to smallest.
  2. Host bits = the smallest n where 2n − 2 ≥ hosts.
  3. Prefix = 32 − n. That is the subnet size.
  4. Place it at the next free address that is aligned to its own block size.
  5. Repeat. If a block does not fit, the plan is over-committed.
Base prefix
Split into
/
 
Why /64 is the default LAN size
  • SLAAC needs 64 host bits, so every LAN is a /64 even if it has five devices.
  • One /48 gives you 65,536 /64 LANs — that is the site allocation.
  • Subnet bits are the bits between the site prefix and /64. Change those, never the interface ID.

Accuracy notes

  • Binary is shown per bit, with the network portion and the host portion in different colours.
  • The network address is a real 32-bit AND, and the table shows every step.
  • IPv6 compression follows RFC 5952: longest zero run, first one on a tie, used only once.
  • Address type comes from the real prefix, not from the first octet.
  • Any valid address works — the results are never limited to a fixed sample.

How to use it while studying

  1. Before you calculate by hand, predict the network and broadcast.
  2. Type the address into the calculator.
  3. Compare. If you were wrong, look at the AND table and find the bit you got wrong.
  4. Do five problems in the Practice tab. Aim for five correct in a row.
  5. Move the prefix by one (/24 → /25 → /26) and watch which field halves.
  6. Design a VLSM plan for 10.0.0.0/24 by hand, then check it in the VLSM tab.
  7. Take a /48 and split it into /64s on paper, then confirm the first ten in the IPv6 Split tab.

The goal is not to use the calculator forever. The goal is that after 50 problems you no longer need it — and you can explain every field on the screen.

05 · IPv6 Essentials

You cannot avoid IPv6 anymore. Cloud providers hand it out by default, mobile carriers run it, and every certification expects it. Good news: the concepts are the same. Only the notation and a few mechanisms change.

Why IPv6 exists

IPv4 has about 4.3 billion addresses. That ran out. NAT stretched it for decades, but NAT breaks end-to-end connectivity, complicates VoIP and peer-to-peer, and does not scale to billions of devices.

IPv6 has 340 undecillion addresses (2^128). Enough to give every grain of sand an address.

The address format

Eight groups of four hex digits, separated by colons.

2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334

Two compression rules

  1. Drop leading zeros in each group: 0db8 → db8, 0000 → 0.
  2. Replace one run of all-zero groups with :: — only once per address.
2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001
-> 2001:db8::1

The /64 rule

A standard LAN is a /64. That leaves 64 bits for hosts — more than enough for SLAAC. Do not use longer prefixes for LANs; SLAAC requires /64.

Address types

Prefix Type Use
2000::/3 Global unicast routable on the Internet
fe80::/10 Link-local every interface, auto-generated, not routed
fc00::/7 Unique local (ULA) like RFC1918 private space
ff00::/8 Multicast replaces broadcast
::1/128 Loopback localhost
::/0 Default route everything else

There is no broadcast in IPv6. Multicast (and anycast) replace it.

Common multicast addresses:

Address Meaning
ff02::1 all nodes on the link
ff02::2 all routers on the link
ff02::5 OSPFv3 routers
ff02::1:ff00:0/104 solicited-node (used by NDP)

How a host gets an address

Two mechanisms, often both:

1. SLAAC (Stateless Address Autoconfiguration)

  • Host sends a Router Solicitation to ff02::2
  • Router replies with a Router Advertisement containing the /64 prefix
  • Host builds its own address (EUI-64 or privacy extension) and does Duplicate Address Detection

2. DHCPv6

  • Stateful: server assigns addresses (like DHCPv4)
  • Stateless: server only gives DNS and other options; address comes from SLAAC

Most enterprise networks use SLAAC + stateless DHCPv6 or DHCPv6 stateful, depending on the vendor and policy.

NDP replaces ARP

Neighbor Discovery Protocol does what ARP, ICMP redirect, and router discovery did in IPv4.

Message Purpose
Router Solicitation / Advertisement find routers and prefixes
Neighbor Solicitation / Advertisement resolve a link-layer address (ARP replacement)
Duplicate Address Detection is this address already in use?
Redirect better next hop available

NDP runs over ICMPv6. If you block ICMPv6, you break IPv6. This is the number one IPv6 firewall mistake.

What changed from IPv4

IPv4 IPv6
ARP NDP (ICMPv6)
Broadcast Multicast only
DHCP SLAAC / DHCPv6
NAT everywhere NAT is the exception, not the rule
Header with options Fixed 40-byte header + extension headers
Fragmentation by routers Only the source fragments
Manual/automatic addressing Automatic by design

Dual stack and transition

The practical migration is dual stack: run IPv4 and IPv6 on the same interface.

Cisco:  ipv6 unicast-routing
        interface Gi0/1
         ipv6 address 2001:db8:1::1/64
         ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local

Other transition tools you will hear about:

  • NAT64/DNS64 — IPv6-only clients reach IPv4 servers
  • 6to4 / Teredo — legacy tunnels, mostly dead
  • DS-Lite / MAP-T — carrier-grade IPv4-over-IPv6

Common pitfalls

Pitfall Result
Blocking ICMPv6 NDP breaks, nothing works
Using /48 or /56 on a LAN SLAAC breaks
Forgetting link-local for routing protocols OSPFv3/BGP neighbors fail
Assuming no NAT means no firewall Wrong — stateful firewalls still needed
Using :: carelessly in configs valid but usually means "unspecified"

IPv6 static routes

Static routes in IPv6 work like IPv4, with one prerequisite: routing must be enabled on the device.

ipv6 unicast-routing
ipv6 route 2001:db8:2::/64 2001:db8:12::2
ipv6 route ::/0 2001:db8:12::1
!
ipv6 route 2001:db8:3::/64 GigabitEthernet0/1 fe80::2

A next hop can be a global address or a link-local address. A link-local next hop is not ambiguous only if you also name the outgoing interface, so use the two-part form. Floating statics use a higher administrative distance just like IPv4 and become active only if the preferred route disappears.

show ipv6 route
show ipv6 route static
show ipv6 interface brief
ping 2001:db8:2::10
traceroute 2001:db8:2::10

Common mistakes: forgetting ipv6 unicast-routing, using the wrong prefix length, pointing at a link-local address without an interface, and blocking ICMPv6 in an ACL so neighbour discovery silently fails.

06 · Switching in Depth: VLANs, Trunks, STP

Everything here happens at Layer 2, inside one broadcast domain — or between several of them if you configure it right.

VLANs

A VLAN is a logical switch inside the physical switch. Each VLAN is its own broadcast domain, its own MAC table view, and its own subnet (by convention).

Why they exist:

  • Segmentation — voice, data, guest, IoT, management, each isolated
  • Security — a compromised printer cannot sniff HR traffic
  • Flexibility — move a port to another VLAN with one command
  • Scale — 48 ports split into 6 VLANs without 6 switches
Cisco:  vlan 10
        name USERS
        interface Gi0/5
         switchport mode access
         switchport access vlan 10

Access ports and trunk ports

Port type Carries Connected to
Access One VLAN, untagged end devices (PC, printer, AP)
Trunk Many VLANs, tagged another switch, router, hypervisor, firewall

Trunking uses 802.1Q: a 4-byte tag inserted after the source MAC.

+------+------+--------+------+---------+-----+
| Dst  | Src  | 0x8100 | VLAN | Type    | ... |
|      |      |  (TPID)| (12b)|         |     |
+------+------+--------+------+---------+-----+
  • TPID 0x8100 marks the frame as tagged.
  • VLAN ID 12 bits → 1–4094 usable.
  • Frames on the native VLAN are sent untagged on the trunk.

Native VLAN

By default, untagged frames on a trunk belong to VLAN 1. Best practice:

  • Set native VLAN to an unused VLAN on both ends (must match).
  • Never use VLAN 1 for user traffic.
  • Mismatched native VLANs cause silent cross-VLAN leakage — a real security issue.
Cisco:  interface Gi0/1
         switchport mode trunk
         switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30
         switchport trunk native vlan 999

Always set allowed vlan explicitly. Default is all VLANs, which is how a guest VLAN ends up trunked to a place it should not be.

Inter-VLAN routing

Two ways to route between VLANs:

Method How Use when
Router-on-a-stick (ROAS) router subinterfaces, one per VLAN, over one trunk small sites, lab
SVI (switch virtual interface) L3 switch has an interface per VLAN normal enterprise design
Routed port switch port is a router port (no switchport) core and data center links 
ROAS on the router:
interface Gi0/0.10
 encapsulation dot1Q 10
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0

SVI on a L3 switch:
interface Vlan10
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
ip routing

ROAS has a single trunk as a bottleneck. SVI scales in hardware. Learn ROAS to understand the concept, use SVI in real designs.

Spanning Tree Protocol (STP)

Redundant Layer-2 links create loops. Broadcast frames would circulate forever, MAC tables would thrash, and the network would die in seconds. STP prevents this by blocking redundant ports.

How it works

  1. Elect one root bridge — lowest bridge ID (priority + MAC).
  2. Every other switch picks one root port — the lowest-cost path to the root.
  3. Each segment picks one designated port per segment.
  4. All other ports go to blocking (or discarding in RSTP).
        [Root]
        /    \
      [SW2]--[SW3]      one link is blocked

Port states

802.1D (classic) 802.1w (RSTP) Forwards data?
Blocking Discarding no
Listening Discarding no
Learning Learning no (learns MACs)
Forwarding Forwarding yes
Disabled Disabled no

Classic STP takes 30–50 seconds to converge. RSTP takes under a second. Modern networks run RSTP (802.1w) or MSTP (802.1s). Never design with classic STP.

Cost

Speed STP cost (short mode)
10 Mbps 100
100 Mbps 19
1 Gbps 4
10 Gbps 2

Timers and tuning

  • Hello 2 s, forward delay 15 s, max age 20 s (classic).
  • Set priority 4096 or 0 on the switch you want as root, and never leave it random.
  • PortFast on access ports to skip listening/learning for end devices.
  • BPDU Guard on access ports to shut them down if a switch is plugged in.
  • Root Guard on ports facing other networks to stop a rogue root.
  • Loop Guard on fiber/trunk links to prevent loops from unidirectional failures.

Common STP problems

Symptom Cause
Network freezes on a new cable physical loop, STP disabled or filtered
Root bridge is an old access switch default priority, nobody set the root
Flapping links, TCN storms unstable link or duplex mismatch
Port stuck in blocking wrong cost or priority, or a loop 
Cisco:  show spanning-tree
        show spanning-tree root
        show spanning-tree interface Gi0/1 detail

EtherChannel / LAG

Bundle several links into one logical link for bandwidth and redundancy.

Protocol Notes
LACP (802.3ad) open standard, active/passive, recommended
PAgP Cisco proprietary, desirable/auto
Static (on) no negotiation, fragile — avoid

Requirements: same speed, same duplex, same VLAN config, same trunk settings on all members.

interface range Gi0/1-2
 channel-group 1 mode active
!
interface Port-channel1
 switchport mode trunk

Hashing is per-flow, not per-packet. One TCP connection will not exceed one member link's speed. Do not promise "2 Gbps" to a single server.

Port security

Limit which MACs can use a port.

interface Gi0/5
 switchport port-security
 switchport port-security maximum 2
 switchport port-security violation restrict
 switchport port-security mac-address sticky

Violation modes: protect (drop silently), restrict (drop + log + counter), shutdown (err-disable). Know all three — it is a classic exam and interview question.

Discovery protocols: CDP and LLDP

Protocol Owner Layer Notes
CDP Cisco proprietary Layer 2 On by default, very detailed
LLDP IEEE 802.1AB Layer 2 Vendor-neutral, must usually be enabled 
show cdp
show cdp neighbors
show cdp neighbors detail
show lldp
show lldp neighbors
show lldp neighbors detail

They advertise device name, platform, software version, management address, local port, and remote port. That is wonderful for documentation, topology discovery, and voice deployments (LLDP-MED), and it is also free reconnaissance for an attacker.

no cdp run
interface Gi0/1
 no cdp enable
 no lldp transmit
 no lldp receive

Keep discovery on trusted infrastructure links; disable it toward user ports, guest networks, and untrusted service providers. If you disable it everywhere, you also lose the fastest way to prove what is plugged into which port.

Rapid PVST+ and STP protection

Variant Standard Scope Notes
STP 802.1D One tree Slow, 30 to 50 seconds
PVST+ Cisco One tree per VLAN Load sharing, still slow
RSTP 802.1w One tree Fast convergence, edge ports
Rapid PVST+ Cisco One rapid tree per VLAN Common Cisco campus default
MSTP 802.1s Groups of VLANs Scales well, needs matching regions

RSTP adds alternate and backup port roles and negotiates with neighbours instead of waiting for timers. Edge ports (PortFast) skip listening and learning and go straight to forwarding, which is correct for host ports and dangerous for switch ports.

spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
spanning-tree vlan 10 root primary
spanning-tree portfast default
spanning-tree portfast bpduguard default
!
interface Gi0/24
 spanning-tree guard root
 storm-control broadcast level 20
  • PortFast - only on ports that face end devices.
  • BPDU Guard - err-disables the port if a BPDU arrives. Stops users from plugging in a switch.
  • Root Guard - stops a downstream switch from becoming root.
  • Loop Guard - protects against unidirectional links that would otherwise create a loop.
  • Storm control - rate-limits broadcast, multicast, or unknown unicast flooding.
show spanning-tree summary
show spanning-tree vlan 10
show spanning-tree root
show errdisable recovery
errdisable recovery cause bpduguard
errdisable recovery interval 300

BPDU Guard puts a port into err-disabled state; it does not fix itself. Know how to recover it, and know why it happened before you re-enable the port.

06B · Wireless LANs

Wireless is a shared medium

An Ethernet switch gives every port its own collision domain. A wireless access point gives every client one shared radio channel, so the rules are different.

  • Half duplex. A radio cannot transmit and receive on the same channel at the same time.
  • CSMA/CA. Listen first, wait a random backoff, transmit, then wait for an ACK. Collisions are avoided rather than detected.
  • Hidden node. Two clients can hear the AP but not each other. RTS/CTS reserves the medium so they stop talking over each other.
  • Interference. Microwave ovens, Bluetooth, cordless phones, neighbouring networks, and metal shelving all raise the noise floor.
  • Rate is per client. A distant client negotiates a lower data rate and holds the channel longer, which slows everyone else.

Signal is measured as RSSI in dBm. Rules of thumb: -30 dBm is excellent, -67 dBm is a common voice threshold, -75 dBm is weak, and -80 dBm is barely usable. Every 3 dB doubles the power; every 10 dB is ten times.

Standards, bands, and channels

Standard Name Bands Notes
802.11b - 2.4 GHz 11 Mbps, very old, interferes with everything
802.11g - 2.4 GHz 54 Mbps, backwards compatible with b
802.11a - 5 GHz 54 Mbps, less interference, shorter range
802.11n Wi-Fi 4 2.4 / 5 GHz MIMO, up to 600 Mbps
802.11ac Wi-Fi 5 5 GHz wider channels, MU-MIMO downlink
802.11ax Wi-Fi 6 / 6E 2.4 / 5 / 6 GHz OFDMA, better density, 6 GHz in 6E
802.11be Wi-Fi 7 2.4 / 5 / 6 GHz multi-link operation, very wide channels

In 2.4 GHz only channels 1, 6, and 11 do not overlap (North America). In 5 GHz there are many more channels, but some are DFS and require radar avoidance. The 6 GHz band is clean because only newer devices use it.

Channel width is a trade: 20 MHz gives more non-overlapping channels; 40, 80, and 160 MHz give more speed per client but fewer channels to reuse. In a dense office, 20 or 40 MHz is usually the right answer. A design that gives every AP an 80 MHz channel will drown itself in co-channel interference.

SSIDs, APs, and controllers

  • SSID is the network name clients see. It is not a security boundary.
  • BSS is one AP radio. Its BSSID is that radio's MAC address.
  • ESS is several APs sharing one SSID so clients can roam. The distribution system (usually the wired LAN) connects them.
  • Roaming is always the client's decision. The network can only make it easier.

An autonomous AP is configured one box at a time. A lightweight AP gets its configuration from a wireless LAN controller (WLC) over CAPWAP (UDP 5246 control, UDP 5247 data). The controller centralises SSIDs, security, RF profiles, and roaming policy.

Fast roaming uses 802.11k (neighbour reports), 802.11v (BSS transition), and 802.11r (fast BSS transition). Voice and video need 802.11r; without it, a roam can drop a call.

A controller can switch traffic centrally or locally at the AP (FlexConnect). Local switching keeps guest and branch traffic off the WAN, but policy has to be applied at the edge.

Wireless security

Mode How it works Use it?
Open No encryption Only with a captive portal or OWE
WEP Broken RC4 key Never
WPA / TKIP Deprecated No
WPA2-Personal Pre-shared key, AES-CCMP Home and small office
WPA2-Enterprise 802.1X with RADIUS, per-user login Business
WPA3-Personal SAE, forward secrecy Preferred for new deployments
WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit mode, 802.1X High-security environments

A pre-shared key is shared by everyone. One leaked laptop and the whole network is compromised. 802.1X gives each user their own credentials and a RADIUS server decides who gets on. EAP-TLS uses certificates; PEAP-MSCHAPv2 uses a username and password inside a TLS tunnel.

Other basics: separate guest SSID on its own VLAN with client isolation, disable WPS, enable management frame protection (802.11w), keep controller and AP firmware current, and watch for rogue APs.

Configuring a WLC

Names differ between AireOS and Catalyst 9800, but the sequence is the same:

  1. Create or confirm the VLAN interface the WLAN will use (for example vlan10).
  2. Create the WLAN with an SSID and a profile name.
  3. Map the WLAN to the interface so client traffic lands on the right VLAN.
  4. Set security: WPA2 or WPA3, PSK or 802.1X, and the RADIUS servers if used.
  5. Enable the WLAN, then verify a client can join and get a DHCP address.
config wlan create 1 CORP CORP
config wlan security wpa akm psk set-key ascii 0 ChangeThisPassphrase
config wlan interface 1 vlan10
config wlan enable 1
show wlan summary
show ap summary
show client summary

That is AireOS-style syntax; Catalyst 9800 uses policy profiles and tags in the GUI or wireless configuration mode. The concept mapping is identical.

The wired side must cooperate: a trunk to the WLC or AP, a DHCP pool for the client VLAN, a default gateway, and DNS. Lightweight APs also need to find the controller, either by DHCP option 43, DNS name CISCO-CAPWAP-CONTROLLER, or a broadcast on the local subnet.

Troubleshooting wireless

Symptom Likely cause Check
Client cannot see the SSID Radio off, wrong band, SSID hidden AP status, channel, broadcast SSID
Association or authentication fails Security mismatch, bad PSK, RADIUS or certificate problem WLAN policy, client supplicant, RADIUS logs, clock skew
Connected but no IP address Wrong VLAN, missing trunk, DHCP or gateway problem Client VLAN mapping, trunk, DHCP pool, show interfaces trunk
Slow for everyone Weak coverage, co-channel interference, low rates, too many clients RSSI and SNR, channel utilisation, retry counters, client count per AP
Drops while walking Coverage gap, sticky client, no fast roaming AP overlap, 802.11r/k/v, roam logs
Intermittent failures Interference, PoE budget, AP reboot Spectrum analysis, show power inline, AP logs

Start at Layer 1: is the AP powered, is the channel clean, is the client close enough? Then Layer 2: did it associate and authenticate? Then Layer 3: did it get an address and a gateway? Most "Wi-Fi problems" are actually VLAN, DHCP, or DNS problems wearing a Wi-Fi costume.

Useful commands (platform dependent): show ap summary, show ap auto-rf, show client summary, show wireless client summary, and the controller's client detail page for RSSI, SNR, retries, and data rate.

07 · Routing Fundamentals

Routing is the act of choosing a path for a packet between networks. Everything else — OSPF, BGP, MPLS — is just a way to fill the routing table.

The routing table

Every router keeps a table of destinations and next hops.

Destination        Mask            Next hop        Interface   Metric
0.0.0.0            0.0.0.0         203.0.113.1     Gi0/0       1
10.0.0.0           255.0.0.0       10.1.1.2        Gi0/1       20
192.168.10.0       255.255.255.0   directly connected Gi0/2    0

When a packet arrives, the router:

  1. Looks up the destination in the table.
  2. Picks the most specific match (longest prefix).
  3. If several routes match equally, picks the lowest administrative distance.
  4. Among routes from the same protocol, picks the lowest metric.
  5. Rewrites the Layer-2 header and forwards.

Longest prefix match

Routes:  10.0.0.0/8  -> via A
         10.1.0.0/16 -> via B
Packet to 10.1.2.3  -> matches both -> /16 wins -> via B

Specificity always beats distance. This is why a host route (/32) can override everything.

Administrative distance

Trust ranking between sources of the same route.

Source Cisco AD Meaning
Connected 0 interface is up
Static 1 you configured it
eBGP 20 external BGP
OSPF 110 link state IGP
IS-IS 115 link state IGP
RIP 120 legacy
iBGP 200 internal BGP
Unknown 255 never use

Lower is more trusted. A static route beats OSPF by default — occasionally useful, often a trap when a "temporary" static route is forgotten for two years.

Static routes

ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.1.1.2      # next hop
ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 Gi0/1         # exit interface
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.1              # default route
ip route 10.9.0.0 255.255.0.0 10.1.1.9 200        # floating static, AD 200

Floating static — a backup route with a higher AD. It sits unused until the primary disappears. Classic WAN design trick.

When to use static routes: stub networks, default routes to an ISP, very small sites, backup paths. Not for anything that changes often.

Default route

0.0.0.0/0 matches everything. It is the "rest of the world" entry.

A router with only directly connected routes and a default route is called a stub router. Most branch sites are stubs.

First-hop redundancy (FHRP)

If the default gateway dies, hosts lose connectivity. FHRP gives them a virtual gateway.

Protocol Vendor Notes
HSRP Cisco active/standby, virtual IP + MAC
VRRP open standard master/backup
GLBP Cisco load balancing across gateways 
interface Vlan10
 ip address 192.168.10.2 255.255.255.0
 standby 10 ip 192.168.10.1
 standby 10 priority 120
 standby 10 preempt

Hosts point at 192.168.10.1 — the virtual address. If the active router fails, the standby takes over. Preempt is what lets the original router take back over when it returns.

Control plane vs data plane

Plane What it does Examples
Control plane decides the path, builds tables OSPF, BGP, STP, ARP
Data plane forwards packets ASIC, TCAM, FIB
Management plane you talk to the device SSH, SNMP, NETCONF

A router can have a correct control plane and a broken data plane (a bug, an ACL, a hardware fault). This is why "the route is there but traffic does not pass" is a real scenario.

Policy-based routing (brief)

Sometimes you must forward based on source, port, or protocol, not destination.

route-map PBR permit 10
 match ip address 101
 set ip next-hop 10.1.1.5
!
interface Gi0/1
 ip policy route-map PBR

Useful for forced inspection or dual-ISP tricks. Use sparingly — it breaks the "routing is destination-based" mental model and confuses everyone later.

Troubleshooting routing

Check Command
Is the route present? show ip route 10.1.2.3
Which protocol installed it? show ip route (code letter)
Is the next hop reachable? show ip arp 10.1.1.2, ping
Is an ACL dropping it? show ip access-lists, counters
Is it asymmetric? traceroute both directions

Asymmetric routing is a favourite interview topic: the reply takes a different path than the request. Usually fine for routing, fatal for stateful firewalls (they see only half the flow and drop it).

08 · OSPF

OSPF is the most common interior routing protocol in enterprise networks. It is a link-state protocol: every router builds a complete map of the area and computes shortest paths with Dijkstra.

The idea in one paragraph

Each router describes its own links (who I am, who I am connected to, what it costs). Those descriptions are flooded to every router in the area. Every router ends up with the same map (the link-state database). Each router then runs the same algorithm on the same map, so everyone agrees on the best path. No rumours, no counting to infinity.

Neighbors first

Before any routing happens, two routers must become neighbors.

Packet type Purpose
Hello "I am here", keeps the adjacency alive
DBD summary of my database
LSR / LSU / LSAck request, send, acknowledge details

Hello timers must match:

Network type Hello Dead
Broadcast (Ethernet) 10 s 40 s
Point-to-point 10 s 40 s
NBMA 30 s 120 s

If hello/dead, area ID, authentication, or subnet do not match, the adjacency stays down.

Neighbor states

Down -> Init -> 2-Way -> ExStart -> Exchange -> Loading -> Full
  • 2-Way is normal between two non-DR routers on a broadcast segment.
  • Full means databases are synchronized.
  • Stuck in ExStart usually means an MTU mismatch.

DR and BDR

On a broadcast segment with many routers, everyone would form a full adjacency with everyone else (n² adjacencies). Instead, they elect a Designated Router and a Backup DR, and everyone syncs with those two.

  • Election: highest priority wins, then highest router ID.
  • Priority 0 means "never become DR".
  • Non-preemptive: a new router with higher priority does not take over until the DR fails.
Cisco:  show ip ospf neighbor
        show ip ospf interface Gi0/1

Areas

Large flat networks are hard to compute and unstable. OSPF splits them into areas.

  • Area 0 (backbone) — all other areas must connect to it.
  • Normal area — full LSDB for its own area, summaries for the rest.
  • Stub / totally stubby — no external routes (or no summaries either). Smaller tables.
  • NSSA — stub but can import external routes as type 7.
        Area 1 --- Area 0 --- Area 2
                     |
                   ABR

ABR (Area Border Router) connects areas. ASBR injects external routes.

Every area must touch Area 0, directly or through a virtual link (avoid virtual links; they are a design smell).

LSAs you must know

Type Name Origin
1 Router LSA every router, its links
2 Network LSA DR, the broadcast segment
3 Summary LSA ABR, prefixes between areas
4 ASBR Summary ABR, how to reach an ASBR
5 External LSA ASBR, redistributed routes
7 NSSA External ASBR inside an NSSA

Types 1 and 2 build the map. Types 3–5 tell you what is outside.

Cost

cost = reference bandwidth / interface bandwidth

Default reference is 100 Mbps, so a 1 Gbps link costs 1 and a 10 Gbps link also costs 1. That is why modern networks change the reference:

router ospf 1
 auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000

Or set it manually:

interface Gi0/1
 ip ospf cost 10

Lower cost wins. Cost is cumulative along the path.

Configuration, minimal

router ospf 1
 router-id 1.1.1.1
 network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
 network 10.1.0.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
 passive-interface Gi0/2
!
interface Gi0/1
 ip ospf 1 area 0

Always set an explicit router ID. Passive interfaces on links with no neighbors (users, loopbacks) — a classic hardening step.

Same lab in FRR:

router ospf
 ospf router-id 1.1.1.1
 network 10.0.0.0/24 area 0

Convergence

When a link fails:

  1. Dead timer expires (40 s by default) or the interface goes down immediately.
  2. The router floods a new LSA.
  3. Every router recomputes SPF.
  4. New routes install.

Tuning for faster convergence: BFD (sub-second failure detection), fast hellos, event-driven SPF. Do not tune timers before you understand them — flapping adjacencies are worse than slow convergence.

Troubleshooting table

Symptom Check
Neighbor stuck in INIT one-way communication, ACL, or multicast blocked
Stuck in 2-WAY normal on broadcast between non-DR routers
Stuck in EXSTART MTU mismatch on the link
Stuck in LOADING corrupt or missing LSA, retransmission
Route missing area mismatch, passive interface, network statement wrong
Route present but no traffic ACL, asymmetric path, or a duplicate router ID
Flapping adjacency bad link, duplex mismatch, CPU overload 
show ip ospf neighbor
show ip ospf database
show ip ospf interface brief
show ip route ospf
debug ip ospf adj        # use carefully, it is verbose

Design rules that save you later

  1. One area 0, keep it small and stable.
  2. Summarize at ABRs (area 1 range 10.10.0.0 255.255.0.0).
  3. Never run OSPF on user-facing ports (passive-interface default).
  4. Set router IDs manually and document them.
  5. Keep the topology shallow; OSPF is not a WAN design tool for 500 sites.

09 · BGP

BGP is the routing protocol of the Internet and of every large enterprise. It does not find the shortest path. It implements policy: who is allowed to reach what, through whom.

If OSPF asks "what is the fastest road?", BGP asks "which road am I contractually and politically allowed to use?"

Autonomous Systems

An AS is a network under one administrative control, identified by a number.

  • Public ASN: assigned by a registry (e.g. 13335 Cloudflare)
  • Private ASN: 64512–65534 (and 4200000000–4294967294 for 32-bit)
AS 65001 ---- AS 65002 ---- AS 65003
   eBGP          eBGP
  • eBGP — between different ASes. Default TTL 1, next hop changes.
  • iBGP — inside one AS. Full mesh required, next hop does not change by default.

Why iBGP needs full mesh or route reflectors

BGP does not re-advertise a route learned from one iBGP peer to another (loop prevention). So with n routers you need n(n−1)/2 sessions. At 20 routers that is 190 sessions.

Solutions:

  • Route reflector (RR) — one router reflects routes to clients.
  • Confederation — split the AS into sub-ASes.

In practice: route reflectors, always.

The BGP session

BGP runs over TCP port 179. It does not discover neighbors — you configure them.

Neighbor states:
Idle -> Connect -> Active -> OpenSent -> OpenConfirm -> Established
  • Active means "trying to connect" (counter-intuitive but correct).
  • Established means the session is up and routes are exchanging.
Cisco:  show bgp summary
        show bgp ipv4 unicast summary
        show bgp neighbors 10.1.1.2
FRR:    show bgp summary

Path attributes

A BGP route is a prefix plus a set of attributes.

Attribute Type Meaning
AS_PATH well-known mandatory sequence of ASes the route traversed
NEXT_HOP well-known mandatory where to send traffic
ORIGIN well-known mandatory IGP, EGP, or incomplete
LOCAL_PREF well-known discretionary preference inside the AS (higher wins)
MED optional hint to the neighbouring AS (lower wins)
WEIGHT Cisco proprietary local preference, highest wins, not advertised
COMMUNITY optional transitive tags for policy (e.g. no-export)
ATOMIC_AGGREGATE / AGGREGATOR optional summarization metadata

Best path selection

Cisco's order, simplified. Stop at the first difference.

  1. Highest weight (local only)
  2. Highest local preference
  3. Locally originated (network command, redistribute)
  4. Shortest AS_PATH
  5. Lowest origin (IGP < EGP < incomplete)
  6. Lowest MED
  7. eBGP over iBGP
  8. Lowest IGP metric to the next hop
  9. Oldest route (eBGP only)
  10. Lowest router ID
  11. Lowest neighbor address

Memorise the first six. That covers 95% of real questions.

The most important insight: BGP prefers the path with the fewest AS hops only at step 4. Local preference beats everything except weight — which is why enterprises control outbound traffic with local preference and inbound traffic with AS_PATH prepending or communities.

Basic configuration

router bgp 65001
 bgp router-id 1.1.1.1
 neighbor 10.1.1.2 remote-as 65002
 network 192.168.10.0 mask 255.255.255.0
 !
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  neighbor 10.1.1.2 activate
  neighbor 10.1.1.2 route-map FROM-ISP in
  neighbor 10.1.1.2 route-map TO-ISP out

FRR equivalent:

router bgp 65001
 bgp router-id 1.1.1.1
 neighbor 10.1.1.2 remote-as 65002
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  network 192.168.10.0/24
  neighbor 10.1.1.2 activate

Filtering: the part that actually matters

You never trust a BGP peer. You filter both directions.

Tool Purpose
prefix-list match prefixes and lengths
route-map match and modify attributes
as-path filter match AS paths
community list match tags
maximum-prefix safety limit against leaks 
ip prefix-list PL-OUT seq 10 permit 192.168.10.0/24
!
route-map TO-ISP permit 10
 match ip address prefix-list PL-OUT
!
neighbor 10.1.1.2 maximum-prefix 1000 80 warning-only

Route leaks happen when you advertise prefixes you do not own. The 2008 Pakistan Telecom YouTube outage and the 2021 Facebook outage both came from BGP mistakes. Always filter outbound, always set maximum-prefix.

Useful knobs

Goal Method
Prefer one ISP for outbound higher local preference
Prefer one ISP for inbound AS_PATH prepend to the other
Backup only (no transit) communities from the ISP
Load sharing across two ISPs accept both, let BGP decide per prefix
Faster failover BFD, bgp fast-external-fallover
Prevent loops AS_PATH (built in)

Common failures

Symptom Cause
Session stuck in Active wrong neighbor IP, no route to it, firewall 179
Session flapping MTU, CPU, keepalive mismatch, unstable link
Session up, no routes prefix not in table, network command wrong, filter blocking
Routes received but not installed next hop unreachable, iBGP sync, better path exists
Only one path used BGP picks one best path by default; use multipath
Sudden traffic shift a prefix was withdrawn somewhere upstream 
show bgp summary
show bgp ipv4 unicast
show bgp ipv4 unicast 10.0.0.0/8
show bgp neighbors 10.1.1.2 advertised-routes
show bgp neighbors 10.1.1.2 received-routes

10 · Network Services

Routing gets packets there. Services make the network usable. Most real tickets live here.

DHCP — giving out addresses

DORA:

Client -> DHCP DISCOVER (broadcast)
Server -> DHCP OFFER
Client -> DHCP REQUEST (broadcast, "I accept this one")
Server -> DHCP ACK

Ports: server 67, client 68.

What DHCP can hand out: IP, mask, gateway, DNS servers, NTP, TFTP, domain name, lease time.

Example pool (Cisco)

ip dhcp pool LAN-10
 network 10.0.0.16 255.255.255.240
 default-router 10.0.0.17
 dns-server 10.0.0.53
 lease 0 8

network takes the network address and subnet mask, not a usable host address. default-router is the router interface clients use as their gateway.

DHCP relay

Broadcasts do not cross routers. If the server is on another subnet, the router acts as a relay agent (ip helper-address 10.1.1.10 on Cisco). It rewrites the request with the giaddr field so the server knows which pool to use.

Symptom Cause
Host gets 169.254.x.x no DHCP response at all
Wrong subnet leased relay missing or pointing at the wrong interface
Some hosts work, some do not pool exhausted, or VLAN mismatch
Lease renews but DNS missing option 6 not configured 
Cisco:  show ip dhcp binding
        show ip dhcp pool
        show ip dhcp conflict

DHCP snooping — a switch feature that only trusts DHCP offers from uplink ports. Without it, anyone can run a rogue DHCP server and become the gateway. Tie it to IP Source Guard and Dynamic ARP Inspection for a real defence.

DNS — names to addresses

Resolution flow for www.example.com:

1. Host checks its cache, then /etc/hosts
2. Asks its configured resolver (recursive query)
3. Resolver checks cache; if miss, walks the tree:
   root -> .com -> example.com -> www.example.com   (iterative)
4. Returns the A/AAAA record, cached for the TTL
Record Meaning
A IPv4 address
AAAA IPv6 address
CNAME alias to another name
MX mail server
NS authoritative nameserver
TXT SPF, DKIM, verification
PTR reverse lookup
SRV service location

TTL is the cache lifetime. Lowering TTL before a migration is standard practice; forgetting it is why "the change did not take effect" for hours.

Common tools:

dig example.com
dig +short example.com
dig @8.8.8.8 example.com
dig +trace example.com        # follow the delegation chain
nslookup example.com          # Windows

Why DNS breaks networks: if DNS fails, users say "the internet is down" even though routing is perfect. Always test by IP before blaming the network.

NAT — translating addresses

Type What it does
Static NAT one private ↔ one public, permanent
Dynamic NAT pool of public addresses
PAT / NAT overload many private → one public, by source port
NAT64 IPv6 ↔ IPv4 
ip nat inside source list 10 interface Gi0/0 overload
interface Gi0/1
 ip nat inside
interface Gi0/0
 ip nat outside

Static mappings and pools

ip nat inside source static 10.0.0.10 203.0.113.10
!
access-list 10 permit 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255
ip nat pool PUBLIC 203.0.113.20 203.0.113.30 netmask 255.255.255.240
ip nat inside source list 10 pool PUBLIC overload
!
show ip nat translations
show ip nat statistics
clear ip nat translation *

Use static NAT when an inside server must be reachable from outside. A pool with overload gives you several public addresses but still shares them by port, which is what most small networks actually need.

NAT breaks things that embed IP addresses in payloads: SIP, FTP active mode, some VPNs, IPsec without NAT-T. If a protocol "works internally but not externally", suspect NAT.

NAT also destroys end-to-end addressability, which is why IPv6 exists.

NTP — time

Time is not cosmetic. Certificates, logs, Kerberos, and correlation all depend on it.

  • Port 123/UDP
  • Stratum 0 = atomic clock, 1 = directly attached, 2+ = synced downstream
  • A server at stratum 16 is unsynchronized
Cisco:  ntp server 10.1.1.10 prefer
        show ntp status
Linux:  chronyc tracking
        timedatectl

A wrong clock causes TLS failures and login failures. It is one of the most common "impossible" bugs.

Syslog — logs

Port 514/UDP (or 6514/TLS).

Severity Name
0 Emergency
1 Alert
2 Critical
3 Error
4 Warning
5 Notification
6 Informational
7 Debugging 
logging host 10.1.1.20
logging trap informational
logging buffered 16384

Send logs to a central server. Logs on the device disappear when the device dies — which is exactly when you need them.

SNMP — monitoring

Version Security
v1 community string, plaintext
v2c community string, plaintext, bulk
v3 users, authentication (SHA), encryption (AES)

Ports 161/UDP (poll) and 162/UDP (trap). Use v3 and read-only in production. Poll with a monitoring system (LibreNMS, Zabbix, Prometheus snmp_exporter) and alert on interface errors, CPU, uptime, and BGP state.

QoS — when bandwidth is not enough

Four steps, in order:

  1. Classify — identify traffic (ACL, NBAR, DSCP)
  2. Mark — set DSCP/CoS at the edge, trust it in the core
  3. Queue — priority queue for voice, weighted queues for the rest
  4. Shape/police — smooth or drop excess
DSCP Typical use
EF (46) voice
AF41 (34) video
AF31 (26) call signalling
CS1 (8) scavenger / bulk
0 best effort

Police drops or marks above a rate. Shape buffers above a rate. Voice needs low jitter and low loss; bulk data tolerates delay but needs bandwidth.

Rule: QoS cannot create bandwidth. It only decides who suffers first.

Backup and restore configurations

Configuration backups are not optional. A device without a recent backup turns a five-minute mistake into an afternoon.

copy running-config startup-config
copy running-config tftp://10.0.0.50/R1.cfg
copy tftp://10.0.0.50/R1.cfg running-config
!
archive
 path tftp://10.0.0.50/$h-archive
 write-memory
show archive
configure replace tftp://10.0.0.50/R1.cfg force

TFTP sends everything in clear text and has no authentication. Use SCP or SFTP in production, restrict access to the backup server with an ACL, and keep copies off the device. The archive feature keeps timestamped versions on the device or a server and works with configure replace for a controlled rollback.

Verify a restore, do not assume it: compare the candidate with the running config, apply it, check interfaces and routing neighbours, then save. Store configs in Git if you can. A diff is worth more than a filename like final-final-v3.cfg.

11 · Network Security

You are not expected to be a penetration tester. You are expected to build a network that does not fall over when someone plugs in a laptop.

The threat model, briefly

Threat Example Control
Reconnaissance port scans, ping sweeps filtering, no unnecessary exposure
Credential theft weak SNMP/community strings, telnet SSH, SNMPv3, AAA
Lateral movement flat network, one VLAN for everything segmentation, ACLs
Spoofing ARP/DHCP/IP spoofing DAI, DHCP snooping, uRPF
Denial of service flood, SYN flood rate limits, upstream scrubbing
Data in transit unencrypted management TLS, IPsec, SSH
Insider misconfiguration, rogue device port security, 802.1X, logging

The biggest real-world risk is a flat network: everything in one VLAN, one subnet, no policy. One compromised printer means everything is reachable.

ACLs

An access list is an ordered list of permit/deny rules. First match wins. There is an implicit deny at the end.

Standard vs extended

Type Matches Number range (Cisco)
Standard source IP only 1–99, 1300–1999
Extended source, destination, protocol, ports 100–199, 2000–2699 
access-list 100 permit tcp 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 443
access-list 100 permit tcp 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 80
access-list 100 deny ip any any log

Apply it:

interface Gi0/0
 ip access-group 100 in

Direction matters. in filters traffic entering the interface from the attached network. out filters traffic leaving toward it. Getting the direction backwards is the single most common ACL mistake.

Wildcard masks

An ACL mask is the inverse of a subnet mask.

Subnet mask Wildcard
255.255.255.0 0.0.0.255
255.255.255.128 0.0.0.127
255.255.255.252 0.0.0.3
255.255.0.0 0.0.255.255 
permit 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255   # whole /24
permit 10.1.1.5 0.0.0.0     # one host
permit any                  # everything

Where to place ACLs

  • Extended ACLs close to the source — stop traffic early, save bandwidth.
  • Standard ACLs close to the destination — they only match source, so placing them early blocks the wrong things.

Stateful vs stateless

Criteria Stateless (ACL) Stateful (firewall)
Remembers connections no yes
Return traffic must be allowed explicitly automatically allowed
Asymmetric routing tolerates it breaks

A firewall builds a session table from the 5-tuple. That is why it can allow replies without an inbound rule — and why it drops traffic when the reply takes a different path.

Zones and DMZ

Internet --- [ outside ] --- FIREWALL --- [ inside ] --- Users
                                  |
                              [ dmz ] --- Public servers
Zone Trust Contains
Outside untrusted Internet
DMZ semi-trusted web, mail, reverse proxies
Inside trusted users, internal apps

Rules of thumb:

  • Inside → outside: allow, with web filtering
  • Outside → DMZ: only the published ports
  • DMZ → inside: deny (this is the one people forget)
  • Management: separate VLAN, not reachable from users

VPN

IPsec (site-to-site)

Two phases:

Phase Purpose Ports
IKE phase 1 authenticate peers, build a secure channel UDP 500 (4500 with NAT-T)
IKE phase 2 negotiate the actual data tunnel (ESP) ESP (protocol 50)

Components to match on both sides:

  • Encryption (AES-256)
  • Integrity (SHA-256)
  • DH group
  • Authentication (PSK or certificates)
  • Interesting traffic (the subnets in the crypto ACL)
  • Lifetime

A single mismatch means the tunnel never comes up. When troubleshooting, compare the full proposal on both sides, line by line.

Cisco:  show crypto isakmp sa
        show crypto ipsec sa
        show crypto session

SSL/TLS VPN (remote access)

Client connects to a portal over 443, authenticates, and gets a tunnel or per-app proxy. Works through almost any firewall because it looks like HTTPS.

WireGuard

Modern, simple, fast. UDP only, no built-in user authentication — pair it with a proper identity system. Great for site-to-site and admin access.

802.1X — port-based authentication

Before a device gets network access, it must authenticate.

Supplicant (PC) <--EAPOL--> Authenticator (switch) <--RADIUS--> Authentication server
  • Port starts in an unauthorized state.
  • EAP exchange happens.
  • RADIUS returns Accept/Reject and often a dynamic VLAN.
  • MAB (MAC Authentication Bypass) for devices that cannot do 802.1X (printers, cameras).

RADIUS ports: 1812 (auth), 1813 (accounting).

This is how you stop someone plugging an unknown laptop into a wall port.

Layer-2 hardening checklist

Management plane hygiene

Do Do not
SSH v2 with keys Telnet, SNMPv1/v2c
AAA with per-user accounts shared admin/admin
Out-of-band management network management on the user VLAN
Logging to a central server logs only in RAM
Config backups automated "I have it in my laptop"
NTP everywhere manual clocks

Hardening device access

Most breaches do not start with a zero-day. They start with Telnet, a shared password, or an admin interface exposed to the internet.

hostname R1
enable secret StrongEnough#2026
service password-encryption
!
username netadmin privilege 15 secret AnotherStrong#2026
ip domain-name example.com
crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
ip ssh version 2
!
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh
 exec-timeout 10 0
 access-class 20 in
!
access-list 20 permit 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255
access-list 20 deny any
!
no ip http server
no ip http secure-server
banner motd ^C Authorized access only. Disconnect now if you are not authorized. ^C
login block-for 120 attempts 3 within 60
  • enable secret is hashed; enable password is not. Use secret, always.
  • service password-encryption only obfuscates weak passwords. It is not encryption.
  • Restrict VTY access with an ACL, use SSH v2, and set an idle timeout.
  • login block-for slows brute force but is not a substitute for strong credentials.
  • Use AAA (TACACS+ or RADIUS) for per-user accountability. Local accounts are a fallback.
  • Privilege levels and role-based views limit what a junior operator can break.

Test it: connect with SSH from an allowed host, confirm Telnet is refused, confirm a bad password is logged, and confirm the ACL blocks an unlisted address.

Security program elements and password policy

Technology is only part of security. A program also needs people, process, and physical controls.

  • Awareness and training - phishing, social engineering, safe handling of data.
  • Physical security - locked comms rooms, console access control, badge logs, camera coverage.
  • Policies and procedures - acceptable use, incident response, change management, offboarding.
  • Least privilege - the minimum access for the job, reviewed regularly.
  • Backups and recovery - tested restores, offline copies, documented recovery time.
  • Patching - a schedule and an owner, not a wish.
  • Monitoring - central logs, alerts, and someone who reads them.
  • Third-party risk - vendors with access are part of your attack surface.

A workable password policy: at least 12 characters or a passphrase, unique per account, stored in a password manager, multi-factor authentication everywhere it is supported, account lockout after repeated failures, no shared admin accounts, disable accounts on the day someone leaves, and rotate only on evidence of compromise or a documented requirement. Arbitrary 90-day rotation encourages Summer2026! and then Summer2026!!.

These controls are usually driven by a framework: NIST CSF, ISO 27001, CIS Controls, PCI DSS, HIPAA, or SOC 2. You do not need to memorise every clause, but you should know why an auditor asks for logs, backups, and access reviews.

12 · WAN, SD-WAN, and Cloud

The WAN is the part you do not own. That changes everything: cost, latency, and who you call when it breaks.

The old WAN

Technology What it was
Leased line dedicated circuit, expensive, fixed bandwidth
Frame Relay shared, committed rate, obsolete
ATM cell-based, obsolete
MPLS L3VPN provider-managed, any-to-any, QoS, still common

MPLS in one page

The provider builds a private network. Your sites connect to PE routers. The provider adds a label to each packet so core routers forward by label, not by IP lookup.

  • CE = customer edge, PE = provider edge, P = provider core
  • Labels stack; the outer label is the transport, the inner identifies the VPN
  • Traffic engineering and QoS come for free from the provider's SLAs
  • Expensive, slow to change (weeks to add a site)

You configure a plain IP link to the provider and run BGP or static routes with them. The MPLS magic is invisible to you.

The modern WAN: SD-WAN

Instead of one expensive private circuit, use several cheap ones (broadband, LTE, fiber) and let software choose the best path per application.

Feature What it does
Overlay builds tunnels (IPsec, WireGuard, proprietary) over any underlay
Application-aware routing voice goes over the low-latency link, backups over the cheap one
Central policy configure once, push to all sites
Zero-touch provisioning ship a box, it phones home and configures itself
Local internet breakout SaaS traffic goes straight out, not back to HQ

SASE extends this to security: cloud-delivered firewall, CASB, ZTNA, and SWG at the edge instead of a box in a data center.

Trade-off: SD-WAN is only as good as the underlay. If the broadband is congested, no policy can fix it.

DIA vs backhaul

Backhaul:  Branch -> HQ (inspect) -> Internet      slow, expensive, but centralized policy
DIA:       Branch -> Internet (local breakout)     fast, cheap, distributed policy

Most organisations now use hybrid: DIA for SaaS, backhaul/private for sensitive apps.

Cloud networking

Every cloud has the same basic primitives with different names.

Concept AWS Azure GCP
Virtual network VPC VNet VPC
Subnet Subnet (per AZ) Subnet Subnet (regional)
Route table Route table Route table / UDR Route
Internet gateway IGW (implicit) (implicit)
NAT gateway NAT GW NAT GW Cloud NAT
Peering VPC peering VNet peering VPC peering
Hub / transit Transit Gateway Virtual WAN / Hub Network Connectivity Center
Private link to on-prem Direct Connect ExpressRoute Dedicated Interconnect
Stateful firewall Security Group NSG Firewall rules
Stateless ACL NACL (none directly) (none directly)

The mental model that transfers

  1. A VPC/VNet is a routing domain. Subnets are just address ranges inside it.
  2. Security groups are stateful and attached to resources. NACLs are stateless and attached to subnets.
  3. Cloud networks are default-deny for inbound, default-allow for outbound in most providers. That is the opposite of a naive on-prem firewall.
  4. Everything is software-defined. There is no spanning tree, no VLANs, no ARP storms.
  5. Routing is explicit. If a route table does not know a destination, the packet is dropped.

Hybrid connectivity

On-prem ---- (Direct Connect / ExpressRoute) ---- Cloud VPC
On-prem ---- (IPsec VPN over Internet) ---------- Cloud VPC

Design rules:

  • Use BGP for dynamic routing between on-prem and cloud.
  • Never overlap address space. Cloud VPCs make overlap painful and expensive to fix.
  • Two paths minimum, different providers if possible.
  • Put a firewall or inspection VPC between the edge and workloads.

Latency reality check

Path Typical RTT
Same rack < 0.1 ms
Same data center 0.2–1 ms
Same city 1–5 ms
Cross-country 30–70 ms
Cross-continent 150–250 ms
Satellite (GEO) 500–700 ms

Speed of light in fiber is about 200 km/ms, and real paths are not straight lines. If someone promises 5 ms from Manila to Virginia, they are wrong.

2Why does SD-WAN use multiple underlays?

4Why is overlapping address space a disaster in hybrid cloud?
