12B · Network Architectures and Virtualization

Three-tier and spine-leaf

The classic campus design has three layers:

  • Access - ports for users and devices, PoE, VLAN assignment, port security.
  • Distribution - aggregation, inter-VLAN routing, policy, ACLs, and links to the core.
  • Core - fast, simple transport between distribution blocks and the data centre or WAN.

Small sites collapse distribution and core into one pair of switches. That is a collapsed core, and it is normal.

Data centres and large campuses increasingly use spine-leaf. Every leaf connects to every spine; leaves never connect to each other. Traffic between servers (east-west) takes one leaf-spine-leaf hop, and every path is the same length, so ECMP works cleanly. Oversubscription is the design number to watch: if 48 access ports at 10 Gbps share four 40 Gbps uplinks, the ratio is 480:160, or 3:1. Know the ratio before you promise performance.

Layer-2 adjacency across a Layer-3 fabric is delivered with an overlay such as VXLAN with EVPN. The underlay just routes; the overlay carries the VLANs.

SOHO, enterprise, and cloud designs

Design What it looks like Typical use
SOHO One box does routing, switching, Wi-Fi, firewall, DHCP Home, small shop
Enterprise campus Access, distribution, core, WLC, firewalls, WAN edge Office buildings
Branch Small switch and router, often SD-WAN, local internet breakout Retail, clinics
Data centre Spine-leaf, load balancers, firewalls, storage network Servers and applications
Cloud VPC or VNet, subnets, route tables, gateways IaaS, PaaS, SaaS workloads
Colocation Your equipment in someone else's rack and power Interconnect, DR

Traditional WAN used MPLS for private, predictable paths. Modern WAN often uses ordinary internet links plus SD-WAN, which builds encrypted tunnels, steers traffic by application policy, and fails over between links. The design question is not "MPLS or internet" but "which applications need which guarantees, and what does the budget allow?"

Cloud networking is still networking: addresses, routes, gateways, and security rules. The names change and the console is a web page.

Virtualization

A hypervisor runs virtual machines. Type 1 runs on bare metal (ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM); type 2 runs on top of a desktop OS (VirtualBox, VMware Workstation). Servers use type 1.

Each VM has virtual CPUs, memory, disks, and one or more virtual NICs. Those vNICs connect to a virtual switch inside the hypervisor. The physical NICs are uplinks. If the uplink is a trunk, every port group on the vSwitch needs the right VLAN ID, otherwise the VM lands on the wrong network or nowhere at all.

  • A port group is a VLAN plus policy (security, teaming, shaping).
  • MAC learning happens on the vSwitch, so the physical switch must accept multiple MACs on that port.
  • Promiscuous mode is needed for packet capture and some security tools; it is also a risk.
  • Live migration moves a running VM to another host. The network must follow it: same VLANs, same subnets, same policy on the destination.

Virtualisation is why "the server is fine" and "the network is fine" can both be true while the application is broken. The virtual switch sits between them and nobody owns it.

Containers and cloud networking

A container shares the host kernel and packages only the application and its libraries. It starts in milliseconds and is much lighter than a VM. Kubernetes schedules containers across hosts and gives each pod an address; the cluster network is usually an overlay, so the underlay still has to route.

Cloud construct What it does On-premises equivalent
VPC / VNet Isolated virtual network VRF or separate campus
Subnet Address range in one availability zone VLAN and subnet
Route table Where traffic goes next Routing table
Internet gateway Path to the internet WAN edge
NAT gateway Outbound-only internet for private subnets NAT overload
Security group Stateful, instance-level allow rules Host firewall
Network ACL Stateless, subnet-level allow and deny rules Router ACL
Load balancer Distributes traffic across targets ADC or F5

Security groups are stateful: return traffic is allowed automatically. Network ACLs are stateless: you must allow both directions. That single difference explains most cloud troubleshooting tickets.

The shared responsibility model matters. The provider secures the physical facility and the hypervisor; you secure identities, data, operating systems, and the rules you write.

PoE, cabling, and optics

Standard PSE power Typical load
802.3af (PoE) 15.4 W Phones, basic APs, cameras
802.3at (PoE+) 30 W Wi-Fi 6 APs, PTZ cameras
802.3bt (PoE++) 60 W or 90 W Large APs, displays, laptops

Always check the switch's total PoE budget, not just per-port capability. Forty ports at 30 W is 1200 W, which many access switches cannot deliver. show power inline tells you what is allocated and what is left.

  • Cat5e - 1 Gbps to 100 m; 2.5G/5G on short runs.
  • Cat6 - 1 Gbps to 100 m; 10 Gbps to about 55 m.
  • Cat6a - 10 Gbps to 100 m; better shielding, thicker cable.
  • Multimode fibre - OM3/OM4, short to medium distances, cheaper optics.
  • Single-mode fibre - long distances, longer-wave optics, higher cost.
  • DAC - direct-attach copper for short rack connections.

Transceivers must match on both ends: speed, wavelength, and fibre type. A 10G SR optic will not talk to a 10G LR optic over multimode. Bend radius, cable management, and labelling are not decoration; they are why the next person can fix it.

Design checklist

  1. What are the applications, users, and growth numbers?
  2. What redundancy is required: power, uplinks, devices, sites?
  3. What is the PoE budget and the cable pathway?
  4. Where does routing happen, and where does policy happen?
  5. How is the network managed, monitored, and backed up?
  6. What addressing scheme and VLAN plan will still make sense in five years?
  7. What is the failure domain, and what happens when one link or one switch dies?

The most common design mistake is buying hardware before writing the requirements. The second is forgetting management access, out-of-band access, and a rollback plan.

13 · Troubleshooting Like an Engineer

This is the chapter that gets you hired. Anyone can configure a lab. Not everyone can find a problem at 2 a.m. without breaking it further.

The method

Never troubleshoot by trying random things. Use a loop.

1. Define the problem precisely
2. Gather facts
3. Form a hypothesis
4. Test the hypothesis
5. Fix, verify, document
   (if wrong, go back to 3 with new facts)

1. Define the problem

"The network is down" is not a problem statement. Ask:

  • Who is affected? One user, one floor, one site, everyone?
  • What exactly fails? DNS, a specific app, all traffic?
  • When did it start? What changed recently?
  • Is it constant or intermittent?

"What changed?" solves more tickets than any command.

2. Gather facts

Layer Fact Tool
L1 link up? errors? ip link, ethtool, show interface
L2 MAC learned? VLAN? ip neigh, bridge fdb, show mac address-table
L3 route exists? ip route, show ip route, traceroute
L4 port open? ss -tulpn, nc -vz, ACL counters
L7 app responds? curl -v, dig, logs

3. Form a hypothesis

A hypothesis is testable: "The DHCP relay is missing on VLAN 30, so hosts on VLAN 30 get link-local addresses."

Not testable: "It's probably the firewall."

4. Test it

One change at a time. If you change two things, you learn nothing.

5. Fix, verify, document

Verification means the user confirms it works, not "it pings now". Documentation means the next person (probably you at 3 a.m.) can find it.

The tools you actually use

Tool Use Trap
ping reachability, RTT ICMP often blocked; success ≠ app works
traceroute path shows forward path only, per-hop filtering hides hops
mtr path + loss over time shows loss accumulating only where real
dig DNS caching hides problems
tcpdump / Wireshark truth capture point matters — both directions?
ss -tulpn listening ports shows local sockets only
nc -vz host port port test can be blocked by ACLs
curl -v full HTTP/TLS flow do not forget DNS resolution step
show interface / ethtool errors counters reset on reload
show log history time zones differ between devices

Reading show interface output

GigabitEthernet0/1 is up, line protocol is up
  Hardware is ..., address is 0011.2233.4455
  MTU 1500 bytes, BW 1000000 Kbit/sec
  5 minute input rate 12000 bits/sec, 3 packets/sec
  0 input errors, 0 CRC, 0 frame, 0 overrun, 0 ignored
  0 output errors, 0 collisions, 0 interface resets
Field Meaning when non-zero
CRC / FCS bad cable, bad optic, duplex issue
input errors physical layer problem
late collisions duplex mismatch
overrun device cannot keep up
interface resets flapping, power, or line issue
output drops congestion, queue full
runts / giants MTU or bad NIC

up/up means Layer 1 and Layer 2 are fine. It does not mean routing or firewalls are fine.

Capture workflow

  1. Decide the capture point. The right question: "where can I see both directions?"
  2. Use a filter, not a 2 GB file. host 10.1.1.5 and port 443
  3. Reproduce the problem once.
  4. Stop and check counts: SYN sent? SYN-ACK returned? Retransmissions?
  5. Open in Wireshark, apply a display filter.

Useful Wireshark filters:

tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0     # connection attempts
tcp.analysis.retransmission                  # retransmits
icmp.type == 3                               # unreachable
dns.flags.response == 0                      # DNS queries
tls.handshake.type == 1                      # client hello
arp                                          # ARP

Expert Information (Analyze → Expert Information) surfaces retransmissions, resets, and malformed packets without reading every packet.

Ten classic tickets

# Symptom Most likely cause
1 Works by IP, fails by name DNS
2 One VLAN cannot reach anything missing SVI/gateway or trunk allowed list
3 Link up, terrible throughput duplex mismatch
4 Intermittent drops every ~30 s STP topology change or loop
5 New switch plugged in, whole floor dies unmanaged loop, no BPDU guard
6 VPN up, small packets fine, large transfers hang MTU/MSS
7 Some users get 169.254.x.x DHCP pool exhausted or relay missing
8 SG works, SSH to device times out management ACL or out-of-band path
9 HTTPS fails with certificate error clock skew or expired cert
10 BGP session up, no traffic filter, next-hop unreachable, or a better path

Escalation etiquette

When you hand off, give:

  • The exact symptom and impact
  • What you checked and what you ruled out
  • Timestamps (with time zone)
  • Captures and command output
  • What you changed, if anything

"The network is broken, please check" wastes everyone's time.

14 · Automation and Programmability

Every network engineer hired after 2020 is expected to automate. Not because it is trendy, but because a 500-device network cannot be configured by hand without errors.

Why automate

Manual Automated
500 devices × 20 min = 166 hours one script, 10 minutes
typos, missed devices, drift consistent, repeatable
knowledge in one person's head knowledge in Git
change window = all night change window = one hour

The goal is not "replace engineers". It is to stop wasting engineers on copy-paste.

Data formats

YAML

switches:
  - name: sw1
    mgmt: 10.0.0.11
    vlans: [10, 20, 30]
  - name: sw2
    mgmt: 10.0.0.12
    vlans: [10, 20]

JSON

{"switches": [{"name": "sw1", "mgmt": "10.0.0.11", "vlans": [10, 20, 30]}]}

YAML is for humans, JSON for machines. Both map to the same structures: dicts, lists, strings, numbers, booleans.

APIs

REST

GET    /api/devices
POST   /api/devices
PUT    /api/devices/1
DELETE /api/devices/1

Stateless. Authenticate with a token or basic auth. Returns JSON. Learn curl first, then a library.

curl -s -H "Authorization: Token $TOKEN" https://netbox/api/dcim/devices/ | jq '.results[].name'

Status codes you will see

Code Meaning Typical cause
200 OK Successful GET or update
201 Created Successful POST
204 No content Successful DELETE or update with no body
400 Bad request Malformed JSON or missing field
401 Unauthorized Missing or expired token
403 Forbidden Valid login, insufficient role
404 Not found Wrong path or object id
409 Conflict Object already exists or state conflict
429 Too many requests Rate limit; back off and retry
500 Server error Controller or device fault
503 Unavailable Overloaded or maintenance

NETCONF / RESTCONF / gNMI

Protocol Transport Model Use
NETCONF SSH (830) YANG full config, transactions
RESTCONF HTTPS YANG REST-style config
gNMI gRPC YANG streaming telemetry

YANG is the data model — a schema describing what a device can be configured with. This is the "structured data" alternative to screen-scraping CLI output.

Python for network engineers

You need very little Python. This is the whole starting set:

# variables and strings
host = "10.0.0.1"
port = 22
print(f"connecting to {host}:{port}")

# lists and dicts
vlans = [10, 20, 30]
device = {"name": "sw1", "mgmt": "10.0.0.11"}

# loops
for vlan in vlans:
    print(f"vlan {vlan}")

# conditionals
if "mgmt" in device:
    print(device["mgmt"])

# files
with open("inventory.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.strip())

# functions
def backup(host):
    return f"backup-{host}.cfg"

# error handling
try:
    do_something()
except Exception as exc:
    print(f"failed: {exc}")

That is enough to write 80% of useful network scripts.

Libraries, in order of learning

Library What it does When
subprocess run CLI tools always, start here
requests HTTP APIs REST APIs, NetBox
Netmiko SSH to network devices CLI-based devices
NAPALM vendor-neutral config/getters multi-vendor
Nornir parallel automation framework scale
Ansible declarative automation teams, ops
pynetbox NetBox API source of truth
Jinja2 templating configs generate configs

The pattern that matters: source of truth → template → deploy → verify

NetBox (intent)
      |
      v
Jinja2 template  ->  rendered config
      |
      v
Nornir / Ansible  ->  push to devices
      |
      v
Verify + report

Never edit devices by hand after this exists. Change NetBox, run the pipeline, verify.

Example: Jinja2 template

{% for vlan in vlans %}
vlan {{ vlan.id }}
 name {{ vlan.name }}
{% endfor %}

Example: idempotent backup

import subprocess, datetime, pathlib

stamp = datetime.datetime.now().strftime("%Y%m%d-%H%M%S")
out = pathlib.Path("backups") / stamp
out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

for host in ["10.0.0.11", "10.0.0.12"]:
    cfg = subprocess.run(
        ["ssh", host, "show running-config"],
        capture_output=True, text=True, check=True,
    ).stdout
    (out / f"{host}.cfg").write_text(cfg)

Idempotent means: running it twice does not break anything.

Git

Non-negotiable. Your configs and scripts go in Git.

git init
git add .
git commit -m "add ospf lab"
git log --oneline
git diff

Why it matters: every change is attributable, reversible, and reviewable. A network engineer without Git is a network engineer who cannot answer "what changed?".

Safe automation rules

  1. Dry run first. Print what would change before changing it.
  2. One device at a time until the script is proven.
  3. Back up before deploy. Always.
  4. Verify after deploy. Compare the intended state to the actual state.
  5. Blast radius. Never run a loop over all devices on the first attempt.
  6. Rate limit. SSH sessions are cheap; device CPUs are not.
  7. Log everything. Who ran what, on which device, at what time.

Configuration management tools

Tool Agent Language Model
Ansible None (SSH or API) YAML playbooks Push
Puppet Agent Puppet DSL Pull, periodic
Chef Agent Ruby recipes Pull, periodic
Plain scripts None Python, Bash Whatever you wrote

Ansible is usually the first tool network engineers learn because it needs no agent on the device and reads like a task list.

- name: Ensure NTP servers
  cisco.ios.ios_config:
    lines:
      - ntp server 10.0.0.10
      - ntp server 10.0.0.11

Idempotency is the point: run it twice and the second run changes nothing. Keep inventory and variables in Git, render configs from templates, run in check mode, apply to one canary, verify, then roll out. If you cannot roll back, you are not ready to roll out.

What to learn next

  • Terraform for cloud/network infrastructure
  • Streaming telemetry (gNMI) instead of polling
  • CI/CD for network changes (GitHub Actions + tests)
  • Batfish to verify configs before deployment
  • Containerlab to test changes before touching production

14B · Controller-Based Networking and SDN

Why a controller

On a traditional network every device is configured separately. Ten switches mean ten logins, ten chance for drift, and no single view of intent. A controller centralises configuration and policy, watches the whole fabric, and makes changes from one place.

That does not remove the need to understand routing and switching. A controller is a tool that pushes a model; if the model is wrong, it pushes the wrong thing everywhere, faster.

The three planes

Plane What it does Example
Management How you configure and monitor SSH, HTTPS, SNMP, syslog
Control Builds the forwarding table OSPF, BGP, STP, ARP
Data Forwards the actual packets ASIC, TCAM, forwarding table

Traditional devices run all three locally. SDN separates the control plane from the forwarding devices and puts it in a controller. The devices become simpler forwarders that ask the controller what to do.

In practice most enterprise "SDN" keeps distributed control planes (OSPF, BGP, STP still run) and adds centralised management, assurance, and policy. The exam and the job both care about the difference between the marketing and the architecture.

SDN architecture

  • Controller - the brain: topology, policy, path calculation, telemetry.
  • Northbound API - REST or similar, used by applications, orchestration, and your scripts.
  • Southbound API - how the controller talks to devices: OpenFlow, NETCONF, RESTCONF, gNMI, or plain CLI/SNMP for legacy gear.
  • Overlay - VXLAN or similar encapsulation that carries Layer-2 segments over a Layer-3 underlay.

Declarative means "this is the desired end state" (the controller works out the steps). Imperative means "do these commands in this order". Modern APIs and tools are declarative; classic CLI scripts are imperative.

VXLAN encapsulates the original frame in UDP (destination port 4789) with a 24-bit VNI, which gives about 16 million segments. EVPN is the control plane that tells the leaves which MAC and IP addresses live behind which VTEP.

Controller platforms you will meet

Platform What it manages Typical use
Cisco Catalyst Center (formerly DNA Center) Campus switches, wireless, fabric, assurance, images Enterprise campus
Meraki dashboard Cloud-managed switches, APs, security appliances Branch and mid-market
SD-WAN manager WAN edge routers, tunnels, application policy Multi-site WAN
Wireless LAN controller Access points and client policy Any Wi-Fi network
OpenDaylight / ONOS Open-source SDN controllers Labs, research, custom fabrics

A fabric controller typically offers templates, site profiles, device inventory, software image management, and assurance (telemetry plus machine learning to spot anomalies). The value is consistency and visibility, not magic.

Configuration management tools

Tool Agent Language Model
Ansible None (SSH or API) YAML playbooks Push
Puppet Agent Puppet DSL Pull, periodic
Chef Agent Ruby recipes Pull, periodic
SaltStack Agent or agentless YAML / Python Push or pull

Ansible is usually the first tool network engineers learn because it needs no agent on the device and reads like a list of tasks.

- name: Ensure NTP servers
  cisco.ios.ios_config:
    lines:
      - ntp server 10.0.0.10
      - ntp server 10.0.0.11

Idempotency is the property that matters: running the same playbook twice should change nothing the second time. That is what makes automation safe.

A sane workflow: keep inventory and variables in Git, render config from templates, run in check mode, apply to one canary device, verify with show commands or tests, then roll out. If you cannot roll back, you are not ready to roll out.

Learning path

  1. Be solid on VLANs, routing, and STP first. Controllers amplify mistakes.
  2. Learn JSON, HTTP, and REST with curl and Postman.
  3. Try a free DevNet sandbox: read the inventory, GET an interface list, change a description, read it back.
  4. Write a Python script with requests that saves device facts to a file.
  5. Install Ansible, run one playbook against a lab device, then run it twice and prove idempotency.
  6. Read the controller's assurance data and explain one anomaly to a colleague.

You do not need to be a software developer. You need to be a network engineer who can read an API response, use Git, and automate the boring parts without breaking production.

15 · Labs

Twenty labs, in order. Each one has a goal, a tool, and a proof — the thing you show someone to prove you did it.

Do not skip the proof. A lab you cannot demonstrate is a lab you did not learn.

Which labs run in the browser lab? Labs 01, 02 and 04 have starter topologies there. Lab 02 is a routed ping only (no ARP capture), and Lab 04 covers access VLANs only (no trunking). Lab 03 is an IP-calculator drill. Labs 05-20 need Packet Tracer, FRR, Wireshark, a DevNet sandbox or Python; each lab links to the chapter that explains it.

Lab 01 — Two hosts, one switch

  • Goal: ping between two PCs on the same VLAN; read the MAC table.
  • Tool: Packet Tracer
  • Proof: show mac address-table output + explanation of why each MAC is on that port.

Lab 02 — ARP and the gateway

  • Goal: see ARP for the gateway when pinging a remote host.
  • Tool: Packet Tracer simulation mode + Wireshark
  • Proof: capture showing ARP request for the gateway, not for the destination.

Lab 03 — Subnetting drill

  • Goal: 50 random addresses, 100% correct.
  • Tool: pen and paper, then ipcalc
  • Proof: a sheet of worked answers with zero corrections.

Lab 04 — VLANs and trunks

  • Goal: two VLANs, one trunk, inter-VLAN routing with router-on-a-stick.
  • Tool: Packet Tracer
  • Proof: topology + show vlan brief + show interfaces trunk + successful cross-VLAN ping.

Lab 05 — Break the trunk

  • Goal: remove a VLAN from the allowed list and document the symptom.
  • Tool: Packet Tracer
  • Proof: a short table: what you broke, what you saw, how you fixed it.

Lab 06 — STP

  • Goal: three switches in a triangle; find the root, the root ports, the blocked port.
  • Tool: Packet Tracer
  • Proof: show spanning-tree from all three + a diagram of port roles.

Lab 07 — OSPF with three routers

  • Goal: full adjacency, loopbacks reachable, convergence under 10 s.
  • Tool: containerlab + netlab + FRR
  • Proof: show ip ospf neighbor, show ip route ospf, convergence timing.

Lab 08 — Break OSPF

  • Goal: cause and diagnose three failures: area mismatch, MTU mismatch, passive interface.
  • Tool: FRR
  • Proof: for each: the symptom, the state you saw, the fix.

Lab 09 — BGP between two ASes

  • Goal: eBGP session up, loopback advertised, AS_PATH visible.
  • Tool: FRR
  • Proof: show bgp summary + show bgp ipv4 unicast showing the path.

Lab 10 — BGP policy

  • Goal: change outbound preference with local preference, inbound with prepending.
  • Tool: FRR
  • Proof: before/after show bgp output with an explanation of which attribute decided it.

Lab 11 — ACLs and NAT

  • Goal: permit only HTTP/HTTPS out, block the rest, PAT the inside network.
  • Tool: Packet Tracer or FRR + iptables
  • Proof: policy working from two different source hosts + show ip nat translations.

Lab 12 — DHCP and DNS

  • Goal: a DHCP pool with relay, a local DNS record, a client that resolves it.
  • Tool: Linux containers or Packet Tracer server
  • Proof: dig output + DHCP lease table.

Lab 13 — Wireshark deep dive

  • Goal: explain six captures: ARP, ICMP TTL, OSPF hello, BGP open, DNS query, TCP retransmission.
  • Tool: Wireshark
  • Proof: a written "expected / saw / because" list for each capture.

Lab 14 — Automation: config backup

  • Goal: back up every running lab device to timestamped files.
  • Tool: Python
  • Proof: script in Git + a backup directory + one paragraph on error handling.

Lab 15 — Automation: intent to config

  • Goal: YAML inventory → Jinja2 template → rendered config → deployed → verified.
  • Tool: Python + Jinja2 (+ Nornir if you want)
  • Proof: a commit showing the template, the rendered output, and the verification report.

Lab 16 — Wireless SSID, WPA2, and DHCP

  • Goal: Build a working WLAN, join a client, and prove it gets an address from the correct VLAN.
  • Tool: Packet Tracer (WLC or home router) or a real AP you own
  • Proof: Client association screen, DHCP lease, a successful ping, and the WLC client list showing RSSI and the right VLAN.

Lab 17 — Discovery and STP protection

  • Goal: Map neighbours with CDP and LLDP, force a root bridge, and watch BPDU Guard err-disable an edge port.
  • Tool: Packet Tracer or two switches
  • Proof: show cdp neighbors detail, show lldp neighbors, show spanning-tree root, and the err-disabled port after a BPDU is injected.

Lab 18 — IPv6 static routing and SLAAC

  • Goal: Route between two IPv6 networks with static routes and a default route, and let hosts autoconfigure with SLAAC.
  • Tool: Packet Tracer or FRR
  • Proof: show ipv6 route, successful end-to-end ping and traceroute, and a host address learned from the router advertisement.

Lab 19 — NAT static and pool

  • Goal: Publish one inside server with static NAT and give inside clients outbound access through a pool with overload.
  • Tool: Packet Tracer
  • Proof: show ip nat translations before and after traffic, plus a successful outside-to-inside test to the static address only.

Lab 20 — API-driven configuration backup

  • Goal: Pull device facts over RESTCONF, save them to disk, and compare two runs to detect drift.
  • Tool: Python requests, Postman, or a DevNet sandbox
  • Proof: Script, JSON output, and a diff between two runs showing what changed and why.

How to record a lab

Every lab folder should contain:

lab-name/
├── README.md        # goal, topology, what I did, what broke, what I learned
├── topology.yml     # if applicable
├── configs/         # final configs
├── captures/        # pcap files
└── notes.md         # raw observations

The README is what you show in an interview. Write it for a stranger.

Skills get you interviews. Evidence gets you offers.

Criteria Certificate Skill + evidence
Proves you passed a test you can do the work

The practical answer: get one certificate early to pass filters, then build evidence.

Certificate When it makes sense

CCNP Enterprise 2+ years experience, moving to design
Juniper JNCIA / JNCIS Juniper shops
AWS / Azure networking cloud-heavy roles
Vendor-neutral (Network+) absolute beginner, before CCNA

Do not collect certificates instead of building. Three certs and no lab is a red flag.

What employers actually screen for

  1. Can you subnet without a calculator?
  2. Can you explain what happens when you type a URL?
  3. Can you read a packet capture?
  4. Have you broken something and fixed it?
  5. Can you describe a network you built or operated?
  6. Do you document?

The URL question

Practice this until it is fluent:

Browser checks cache → DNS resolution (recursive → root → TLD → authoritative) → TCP handshake to the server IP:443 → TLS handshake (certificate, key exchange) → HTTP GET → server responds → browser renders. Along the way: ARP for the gateway, routing through the default route, NAT at the edge, stateful firewall tracking the session.

Every word in that answer is a chapter in this book.

Portfolio

Three things, in one public repo:

  1. A lab you built — topology diagram, configs, and what you learned.
  2. A capture you explained — the pcap plus your analysis.
  3. A script you wrote — backup, audit, or report. Small is fine.

Add a README.md that says, in plain language, what each one demonstrates.

Interview questions with short answers

Question The answer they want
What happens when you type a URL? DNS → TCP → TLS → HTTP, with ARP/routing/NAT in between
Difference between a switch and a router? L2 vs L3; MAC table vs routing table; one broadcast domain vs boundaries
What is a VLAN? A logical broadcast domain; segmentation without extra hardware
How does OSPF choose a path? Lowest cumulative cost via SPF; DR/BDR on broadcast segments
Why does BGP exist? Policy-based inter-domain routing between autonomous systems
What is the difference between TCP and UDP? Reliability/ordering vs speed/simplicity
How do you troubleshoot "no internet"? Scope, ping by IP, DNS, gateway, ARP, traceroute, capture
What is NAT and why? Address translation to conserve public IPv4; breaks end-to-end
What is an MTU issue and how do you find it? Path MTU discovery failure; test with DF and decreasing sizes
What is your favourite network tool? Be specific and explain why (Wireshark, tcpdump, mtr, Batfish)
Describe a failure you caused and fixed Honesty + method + lesson. This separates candidates
How would you automate 100 switches? Source of truth → template → deploy → verify, with dry runs

Resume bullets that work

Bad: "Responsible for network operations."

Good:

  • "Migrated 42 access switches from static VLAN config to a templated Ansible pipeline, cutting change time from 3 hours to 15 minutes."
  • "Reduced recurring broadcast storms by implementing BPDU Guard and RSTP across 12 buildings."
  • "Built a containerlab lab replicating the production OSPF/BGP design to test changes before deployment."
  • "Documented and automated configuration backups for 120 devices, eliminating manual nightly work."

Formula: action + scale + measurable result.

30-60-90 for a new role

Period Focus
First 30 days learn the topology, the change process, and who to ask; read the docs; do not change anything without a backup
Days 31–60 take small tickets, document as you go, automate one annoying task
Days 61–90 own a change end to end, propose one improvement with data

Where the jobs are

Role Focus
Network operations (NOC) monitoring, tickets, incidents
Network engineer design, build, change
Network automation engineer code + network
Cloud network engineer VPC/VNet, hybrid, transit
Security network engineer firewalls, segmentation, VPN
Solutions architect design and sales support

Start in operations if you can. You will see more failures in one year than a design role sees in five, and failures teach faster than diagrams.

The unfashionable advice that works

  1. Document everything. The engineer who writes the runbook becomes the lead.
  2. Learn one thing deeply. OSPF or BGP or Linux networking — depth transfers.
  3. Read packet captures for fun. It compounds.
  4. Automate the boring part first. Nobody is impressed by a framework; they are impressed by the 15 minutes you gave back.
  5. Be the person who says "let me verify". That is the whole job.

Final check

If all eight are true, you are ready to apply — with or without a certificate.

16B · Device Management

Boot process and files

A router or switch boots in stages: power-on self-test, ROMMON (the tiny bootstrap), load the IOS image from flash, then load the startup configuration into running memory.

show version
show flash:
dir flash:
show boot

The configuration register tells the device where to boot and whether to use the startup configuration. 0x2102 is the normal value. 0x2142 ignores the startup configuration, which is exactly how password recovery works.

show version | include register
configure terminal
config-register 0x2102
end

Startup configuration lives in NVRAM and is copied to RAM at boot. Running configuration is in RAM and disappears on reload unless you save it. That is why copy running-config startup-config is the most important command in this chapter.

Licensing

Modern Cisco IOS XE uses smart licensing, where the device registers with a licensing server or a satellite and reports consumption. Feature sets are enabled by licence level, for example network essentials versus advantage, and DNA tiers for controllers.

show license
show license status
show license summary
license smart register idtoken <token>
license boot level network-advantage

Do not assume a feature is available because the command exists in help. Check the licence. An expired evaluation licence can disable features during a maintenance window, so track expiry before it bites.

Backup and restore

copy running-config startup-config
copy running-config tftp://10.0.0.50/R1.cfg
copy tftp://10.0.0.50/R1.cfg running-config
!
archive
 path tftp://10.0.0.50/$h-archive
 write-memory
show archive
configure replace tftp://10.0.0.50/R1.cfg force

TFTP has no authentication or encryption. It is fine in a lab and unacceptable across an untrusted network. Use SCP or SFTP in production, restrict who can reach the server, and keep backups versioned. A backup you have never restored is a rumour.

For a real restore, compare first: show archive config differences or a text diff against the candidate. Then apply with configure replace, verify with show commands, and save.

Password recovery

Password recovery requires physical or console access. Only do it on equipment you are authorised to recover.

  1. Connect to the console, power cycle, and interrupt the boot to reach ROMMON.
  2. Change the configuration register so the startup configuration is ignored: confreg 0x2142, then reset.
  3. The device boots with no configuration. Enter privileged mode, then copy startup-config running-config.
  4. Set a new enable secret and any missing credentials.
  5. Restore the register to 0x2102, save, and reload.

Check interfaces afterwards. Some platforms administratively shut every interface when they boot without a configuration, and the old config copy may bring back the shutdown state.

Upgrades

  1. Read the release notes and compatibility matrix; pick a target version, not "latest".
  2. Verify the image checksum (MD5 or SHA) before copying.
  3. Confirm free flash space for the new image plus the old one.
  4. Copy the image, set the boot variable, and reload in a maintenance window.
  5. Verify version, interfaces, routing neighbours, and licence after boot.
  6. Keep the old image on flash until the new one has survived a week.
verify /md5 flash:cat9k_iosxe.17.09.04a.SPA.bin
boot system flash:cat9k_iosxe.17.09.04a.SPA.bin
reload
show version

For fleets, use the controller's image management rather than logging into each device. Staged rollout and a golden image beat heroics at 2 a.m.

Monitoring and time

  • NTP - every log, certificate, and correlation depends on correct time. Point devices at internal NTP servers and check show ntp status.
  • Syslog - send to a central server. Severity 0 is emergency, 7 is debug. Never leave production at debug.
  • SNMP - use v3 with authentication and privacy. Poll for trends, trap for events.
  • NetFlow / IPFIX - who talked to whom, how much, and when. Invaluable for capacity and security questions.
  • Configuration drift - compare running config to the intended state on a schedule. Drift is how outages start.
ntp server 10.0.0.10
logging host 10.0.0.20
logging trap informational
show logging
show clock
show ntp status

If you cannot answer "what changed, when, and who changed it", the monitoring is not finished. AAA logging plus configuration backups plus accurate time is the minimum bar.

D · Glossary

Every entry answers three questions: what it is, what it does, and why you should care. If a term has a chapter, the chapter explains it in context.

ACL rules, for example, are not just "permit/deny lists" — they are read top to bottom and stop at the first match, which is why a broad rule near the top makes every rule below it dead.

A

AAA — Authentication, Authorization, Accounting. The three questions asked of anyone who touches the network: who are you, what are you allowed to do, and what did you actually do. RADIUS and TACACS+ are the protocols that carry those answers.

ABR (Area Border Router) — An OSPF router with interfaces in two or more areas. It keeps a separate topology database for each area and advertises summaries between them, so routers inside one area never need to know another area's internals.

ACL (Access Control List) — An ordered list of permit and deny rules attached to an interface or a firewall. The device reads the rules from the top and stops at the first match, so the order is the policy: a broad permit placed too early makes every rule below it useless, and a missing final deny silently allows everything.

Administrative distance — The number a router uses to choose between routes to the same destination learned from different sources. Lower wins: connected 0, static 1, eBGP 20, OSPF 110, IS-IS 115, RIP 120, iBGP 200. It is the tiebreaker applied before metrics are compared.

Ansible — An agentless automation tool that connects over SSH or an API and applies YAML playbooks. Running the same playbook twice should produce the same result, which is what makes it safe.

Anycast — One address assigned to several servers in different locations. Routing delivers each client to the nearest one, which is how 8.8.8.8 and most CDNs work. If one node fails, traffic simply shifts to the others.

AP — The radio that bridges wireless clients onto the wired LAN. In a controller-based network it is lightweight and gets its configuration from a WLC.

ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) — The protocol that finds the MAC address that owns an IPv4 address on the local link. A host broadcasts "who has 10.0.0.1?" and the owner replies with its MAC, which is then cached for a few minutes. Without ARP, a host knows where it wants to go but not which hardware to hand the frame to.

AS (Autonomous System) — A network under one administrative control, identified by an AS number. Routing between ASes is BGP's job; routing inside one AS is an IGP's job.

AS path — The BGP attribute listing every AS a route has passed through. It is both a loop check (seeing your own AS number means reject) and the usual tiebreaker: the shortest path wins unless policy says otherwise.

ASBR (AS Boundary Router) — An OSPF router that connects the OSPF domain to another routing domain and injects external routes into it. A router can be an ASBR and an ABR at the same time; the roles answer different questions.

Automation — Doing configuration and verification with code instead of typing into devices. The value is repeatability: the same input produces the same result, and one mistake is fixed once instead of on two hundred devices.

B

Bandwidth — The maximum rate a link can carry, measured in bits per second. It is a capacity, not a promise: what you actually get is throughput, which is always lower.

BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection) — A lightweight protocol that sends tiny probes every few hundred milliseconds to detect a dead neighbour. Routing protocols use it so they can fail over in under a second instead of waiting for their own slow timers.

BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) — The routing protocol of the Internet. It exchanges reachability between autonomous systems and chooses paths by policy (which path you prefer) rather than by pure shortest path.

BPDU (Bridge Protocol Data Unit) — The message switches exchange to run Spanning Tree. It carries the bridge ID, root path cost, and port information that decide which ports stay forwarding and which get blocked.

BPDU guard — A switch feature that shuts a port down if it receives a BPDU. Applied to access ports, it stops a user from plugging in their own switch and quietly changing the topology.

Broadcast — A frame or packet addressed to every device on the local segment (MAC ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, IPv4 255.255.255.255). Routers do not forward broadcasts, which is exactly what makes a broadcast domain end at the router.

Broadcast address - The last address in an IPv4 subnet, with every host bit set to 1. It reaches every device in that subnet and is never assigned to a host. For 10.0.0.16/28 it is 10.0.0.31.

Broadcast domain — Every device that receives a broadcast sent by any one of them. A whole switch is one broadcast domain unless VLANs split it.

BSS — One access point radio and its clients. Its identifier is the BSSID, the radio’s MAC address; several BSSs sharing one SSID form an ESS.

C

CAM table (Content Addressable Memory) — A switch's map of MAC address to port. The switch learns an entry from every frame's source address and uses the table to send frames out only the correct port instead of flooding.

CAPWAP — The protocol a lightweight access point uses to find and talk to a wireless LAN controller: UDP 5246 for control, UDP 5247 for data.

Chef — A configuration management tool that uses an agent and Ruby recipes to converge devices to a desired state. Like Puppet, it usually pulls policy on a schedule.

CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) — Writing a network as an address plus a prefix length, like 10.0.0.0/8. It replaced address classes, so the prefix defines the size — not the first octet.

Collision domain — The set of devices sharing one physical medium where frames can collide. A hub creates one large collision domain; a switch gives every port its own.

Community (BGP) — A tag attached to a BGP route, such as 65000:100. It has no built-in meaning — you define what it means and match it in route maps to apply policy at scale.

Config register — A 16-bit setting that controls how a Cisco device boots. 0x2102 is normal; 0x2142 ignores the startup configuration, which is used in password recovery.

Control plane — The part of a device that decides where traffic should go: routing protocols, ARP, STP, and the tables they build. It is the "thinking" half of the router.

Convergence — How long the network takes to agree on a new topology after a change and stop sending traffic into a dead path. Fast convergence is a design goal, not a single feature.

CoS (Class of Service) — The 3-bit priority field inside an 802.1Q tag, used for QoS at Layer 2. It travels with the frame across trunks, so switches can honour priority without reading the IP header.

CPE (Customer Premises Equipment) — The device on the customer's side of a provider link, usually the router the ISP installs or hands over. It is where the provider's responsibility ends.

CSMA/CA — Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance. Wireless listens, waits a random backoff, transmits, and waits for an ACK because a radio cannot detect collisions while sending.

D

DAI (Dynamic ARP Inspection) — A switch feature that checks ARP packets against the DHCP snooping table and drops forged replies. It blocks ARP spoofing without installing anything on the hosts.

Data plane — The part of a device that actually moves packets: ASICs, the FIB, and the interfaces. Perfect routes in the control plane mean nothing if the data plane drops the traffic.

Default gateway — The router a host sends traffic to when the destination is not on its own subnet. If it is wrong or missing, local traffic still works and everything else fails — the classic "the network is down but only for me" symptom.

Default route — The route 0.0.0.0/0 (or ::/0), meaning "everything not matched more specifically goes here". It is the last resort in the routing table.

DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) — The protocol that gives hosts an address, mask, gateway, and DNS server automatically. It uses four messages: discover, offer, request, acknowledge.

DHCP pool - A named range of addresses a DHCP server can lease, defined with the subnet's network address and mask plus options such as default-router and dns-server. One pool usually serves one subnet.

DHCP snooping — A switch feature that marks ports trusted or untrusted and accepts DHCP offers only from trusted ports. It stops a rogue server from handing out a fake gateway.

DIA (Direct Internet Access) — Sending a branch's internet traffic straight out a local link instead of back through the data centre. It cuts latency and WAN cost, but moves the security controls to the branch.

DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) — A segment for services that must be reachable from the internet, kept separate from the internal network. If the web server is compromised, the attacker is still outside the inside.

DNS (Domain Name System) — The system that turns names into addresses. Almost every "the internet is down" ticket is really DNS, because everything else depends on it.

DR/BDR (Designated Router / Backup DR) — The two routers elected on an OSPF broadcast segment to be the only ones forming full adjacencies and generating LSAs for that segment. It keeps the number of adjacencies from growing quadratically as routers are added.

DSCP (Differentiated Services Code Point) — The 6-bit field in the IP header that marks a packet's QoS class. Edge devices set it, interior devices trust or rewrite it, and every hop uses it to choose a queue.

Dual stack — Running IPv4 and IPv6 on the same interface at the same time. It is the normal migration method because there is no flag day when the Internet switches over.

Duplex — Whether a link can send and receive at the same time (full) or only one direction at a time (half). A duplex mismatch causes collisions, retransmissions, and terrible throughput on a link that otherwise looks healthy.

E

eBGP — BGP running between routers in different autonomous systems. It is how networks exchange routes with each other, and it is the protocol that builds the Internet's routing table.

EIGRP (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol) — Cisco's advanced distance-vector IGP. It converges quickly and summarizes easily, but it is effectively Cisco-only, which limits mixed-vendor designs.

Encapsulation — Wrapping data in the header of the layer below: a segment gets an IP header, the packet gets a frame header, and the frame becomes bits on the wire. Decapsulation is the reverse process on receipt.

ESS — Several access points sharing one SSID so clients can roam across them while staying on the same network.

EUI-64 — The 64-bit interface ID built from a 48-bit MAC by flipping the universal/local bit and inserting ff:fe in the middle. SLAAC uses it to build an address with no DHCP server.

EVPN (Ethernet VPN) — A BGP-based control plane for Layer-2 and Layer-3 overlays, usually paired with VXLAN. It replaces flood-and-learn with a real routing protocol, which is why large data centres use it.

F

FHRP (First Hop Redundancy Protocol) — A family (HSRP, VRRP, GLBP) that gives hosts one virtual gateway address served by two or more routers. If the active router dies, the standby takes over the address and the hosts never notice.

FIB (Forwarding Information Base) — The data-plane copy of the routing table, optimized for fast lookups. The control plane computes it; the ASIC reads it for every packet.

Floating static route — A static route configured with a worse administrative distance than the primary route, so it stays hidden until the primary disappears. It is a cheap backup path with no protocol overhead.

FRR (FRRouting) — An open-source routing suite that runs OSPF, BGP, IS-IS, and more on Linux. It is what the free labs in this book use instead of vendor images.

G

gNMI — A gRPC-based protocol for reading and changing device state, including streaming telemetry. It is the modern alternative to polling devices with SNMP or scraping the CLI.

GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation) — A simple tunnelling protocol that wraps one protocol inside another. It can carry multicast and routing protocols, which IPsec alone cannot, but it adds no encryption by itself.

H

HSRP (Hot Standby Router Protocol) — Cisco's first-hop redundancy protocol. Routers share a virtual IP and MAC address; one is active, the other stands by and takes over if the active one stops answering.

Hypervisor — The software layer that runs virtual machines. Type 1 runs on bare metal; type 2 runs on a host operating system.

I

iBGP — BGP running between routers in the same autonomous system. It carries external routes inside the AS and needs either a full mesh of sessions or route reflectors.

ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) — IP's signalling protocol. It carries errors such as "destination unreachable" and "time exceeded", plus the echo request/reply that ping uses. It carries no user data.

IGP (Interior Gateway Protocol) — Any routing protocol that works inside one autonomous system: OSPF, IS-IS, EIGRP, RIP. It finds the best path within your network, which is the opposite job to BGP.

IPAM (IP Address Management) — Keeping track of which addresses and prefixes exist and who owns them. Without it, duplicate addresses and exhausted pools are discovered by outage instead of by a report.

IPsec — A suite that encrypts and authenticates IP traffic. It has two parts: IKE negotiates keys and parameters, while ESP (or AH) protects the actual packets.

IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) — A link-state IGP that runs directly on Layer 2 rather than inside IP. It scales very well and is common in ISP and provider cores.

ISP (Internet Service Provider) — The company that sells connectivity to the rest of the Internet.

J

Jitter — Variation in delay between packets. Voice and video care about jitter more than raw latency: a steady 150 ms sounds fine, but 20 ms ± 80 ms does not.

L

LACP (Link Aggregation Control Protocol) — The IEEE standard (802.3ad) for bundling several links into one logical link. It negotiates with the far end, so a half-configured bundle cannot silently create a loop.

Latency — The time a packet takes to travel from source to destination, measured in milliseconds. Distance, queueing, and serialization all add to it.

Link-state — A class of routing protocol where every router builds a complete map of the topology and runs shortest path over it. OSPF and IS-IS are link-state; they converge quickly and scale well.

Local preference — A BGP attribute used inside an AS to choose the outbound path. Highest wins, and it is exchanged only between iBGP peers — it never crosses an AS boundary.

Longest prefix match — The rule that a router forwards by the most specific route, not the first one configured. A /24 always beats a /16 for the same destination.

LSA (Link State Advertisement) — OSPF's unit of topology information. Routers flood LSAs until every router in the area holds the same database, and then each runs shortest path on it.

M

MAC address — The 48-bit hardware address of an interface, used only within one link. It is not routable, and it changes at every hop as frames are rebuilt.

MED (Multi-Exit Discriminator) — A BGP attribute that hints which entry point into an AS is preferred. Lower is better, and it is normally compared only between the same two neighbours.

Metric — The number a routing protocol assigns to a path to rank it. Lower is better, but the meaning differs by protocol: OSPF cost, RIP hop count, EIGRP composite.

MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) — Provider forwarding that attaches a short label to each packet and switches on the label instead of doing an IP lookup at every hop. It is the basis of many carrier VPNs and traffic-engineering designs.

MSS (Maximum Segment Size) — The largest TCP payload a host will accept, usually MTU minus 40 bytes of IP and TCP headers. If a tunnel lowers the MTU, MSS clamping keeps TCP from overrunning it.

MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) — The largest payload an interface will send; 1500 bytes on standard Ethernet. A path with a smaller MTU silently drops large packets unless PMTUD or MSS clamping deals with it.

Multicast — One sender, many receivers, using a group address. Hosts join a group and the network delivers only to links that have members. IPv4 uses 224.0.0.0/4; IPv6 uses ff00::/8.

N

NACL — A stateless, subnet-level allow and deny list in cloud networking. Unlike a security group, you must allow return traffic explicitly.

NAT (Network Address Translation) — Rewriting addresses at a boundary, usually private to public. PAT, also called NAT overload, rewrites the source port too so many hosts can share one public address.

NDP (Neighbor Discovery Protocol) — IPv6's combined replacement for ARP, router discovery, and redirects. It runs over ICMPv6 and also performs duplicate address detection.

NETCONF — A protocol for configuring devices with structured data over SSH. It is transactional: you send a change, the device validates and applies it — or rejects the whole thing.

Network address - The first address in a subnet, with every host bit set to 0. It names the subnet (for example 10.0.0.16/28) and is never assigned to a device.

Next hop — The next device a packet is handed to on the way to its destination. The destination may be far away; the next hop is always exactly one hop away.

NOC (Network Operations Center) — The team and the room where monitoring, alerting, and incident response happen. Their runbooks matter as much as their dashboards.

NTP (Network Time Protocol) — The protocol that keeps clocks synchronized. Log correlation, certificates, and any real troubleshooting all depend on correct time.

O

OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) — A link-state IGP that floods LSAs, builds a topology map per area, and runs Dijkstra to find shortest paths. It is the most common interior protocol in enterprise networks.

Overlay — A virtual network built on top of a physical underlay, usually with tunnels. VXLAN, IPsec, and SD-WAN are overlays: they hide the underlay's details from the tenants.

Oversubscription — The ratio between the bandwidth available to endpoints and the bandwidth available on uplinks. A 48-port 10G switch with four 40G uplinks is 3:1; know the number before promising performance.

P

Packet — The Layer-3 unit of data: an IP header plus payload. Frame is Layer 2, segment is Layer 4, packet is Layer 3.

PAT (Port Address Translation) — NAT that also rewrites the port, letting many internal hosts share one public address. It is what a home router does.

PBR (Policy-Based Routing) — Forwarding decisions based on something other than the destination, such as source address, protocol, or DSCP marking.

PDU (Protocol Data Unit) — The data unit at a given layer: frame at Layer 2, packet at Layer 3, segment at Layer 4.

Peering — Two networks exchanging traffic directly, usually without payment. It is a business relationship expressed as BGP configuration.

Ping — The tool that sends ICMP echo requests and measures the replies. Success proves the path and the return path work; failure does not tell you where it broke.

PMF — 802.11w, which protects wireless management frames such as deauthentication so an attacker cannot forge them. It is mandatory in WPA3.

PoE (Power over Ethernet) — Sending power over the LAN cable with the data, so access points and cameras need no separate supply. Standards run from 802.3af (15.4 W) to 802.3bt (90 W).

Prefix — The network portion of an address, written with its length: 10.1.0.0/16. The prefix length is the number of leading bits that identify the network.

Prefix list — A filter that matches routes by prefix and length. For that specific job it is faster and harder to misconfigure than an access list inside a route map.

Puppet — A configuration management tool that uses an agent and a declarative DSL, with nodes pulling their desired state from a server on a schedule.

Q

QoS (Quality of Service) — Classifying, marking, and scheduling traffic so important packets are served first when a link is congested. It cannot create bandwidth; it decides who suffers when there is not enough.

Queue — A buffer where packets wait for an interface. Queueing is the mechanism behind QoS: which queue is served next is what "priority" actually means.

R

RADIUS — The protocol that centralizes authentication for 802.1X, VPN, and admin logins. The switch or router asks the RADIUS server whether the credentials are good.

Rapid PVST+ — Cisco’s per-VLAN implementation of RSTP (802.1w). It converges in about a second and supports PortFast, BPDU Guard, and Root Guard.

Redistribution — Taking routes learned by one routing protocol and injecting them into another. It is where most routing loops and suboptimal paths are born, so it needs filtering and careful metrics.

RESTCONF — A REST-style protocol for reading and changing YANG-modelled device configuration over HTTPS. It is the HTTP cousin of NETCONF.

ROMMON — The small bootstrap environment a Cisco device uses before loading IOS. It is where you change the config register during password recovery.

Route map — A named list of match/set clauses applied to routes or packets. match selects which items are affected; set changes them.

Route reflector — An iBGP router that relays routes to its clients, replacing the full mesh that iBGP otherwise requires. It is the standard way to scale BGP inside an AS.

Route table — The list of destinations a device knows and where it will send traffic for each one.

Router — A device that forwards packets between networks using Layer-3 addresses. It breaks up broadcast domains and marks where one subnet ends and the next begins.

Routing policy — The rules that decide which routes are accepted, preferred, and advertised. In BGP, policy usually matters more than the protocol's own path calculation.

RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure) — A system that cryptographically certifies which AS is allowed to originate which prefixes. It prevents a whole class of BGP hijacks.

RSTP (Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol) — The 802.1w version of STP, converging in under a second instead of tens of seconds. It is the default on modern switches.

S

SAE — Simultaneous Authentication of Equals. The WPA3-Personal handshake that replaces the WPA2 pre-shared key exchange and provides forward secrecy.

SD-WAN (Software-Defined WAN) — A policy-driven overlay that spreads traffic across several WAN links according to application needs. It replaces static routing over expensive circuits with measured, per-application path selection.

SDN — Software-Defined Networking. Separating the control plane from the forwarding devices and centralising it in a controller, which programs the network through APIs.

Security group — A stateful, instance-level firewall in cloud networking. Return traffic for an allowed connection is permitted automatically.

Segment — The Layer-4 unit: a TCP or UDP header plus payload. The word is also used loosely to mean a piece of a network, so context matters.

Shaping — Delaying packets to keep the rate at or below a limit. Unlike policing, it does not drop traffic; it smooths bursts by buffering them.

SLAAC (Stateless Address Autoconfiguration) — IPv6 hosts build their own address from the prefix a router advertises plus an interface ID. No DHCP server is involved.

Smart licensing — Cisco’s licence model where a device registers with a licensing server and reports consumption instead of using a fixed key per feature.

SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) — The classic protocol for polling counters and receiving traps from devices. Streaming telemetry is replacing it, but it is still everywhere.

Spine-leaf — A data-centre design where every leaf switch connects to every spine switch and leaves never connect to each other. All paths are equal, which suits east-west traffic and ECMP.

SSID — The name a wireless network advertises. It identifies the network to clients but is not a security boundary.

Spanning tree — The protocol that keeps a switched network loop-free by electing a root bridge and blocking redundant ports. Without it, one loop saturates a network in seconds.

Static route — A route configured by hand. It does not adapt to failures unless it is paired with something like BFD or a floating backup.

Storm control — A switch feature that rate-limits broadcast, multicast, or unknown unicast flooding on a port so one loop or misbehaving host cannot saturate the link.

STP (Spanning Tree Protocol) — The IEEE 802.1D protocol that prevents Layer-2 loops. It blocks ports so that exactly one active path exists between any two points.

Subnet — A slice of a larger network, defined by a prefix. Subnetting is the act of choosing where to split the host bits.

Subnet mask — The 32-bit value with 1s in the network bits and 0s in the host bits. The device ANDs it with an address to find the network.

Summarization — Advertising one short prefix instead of many longer ones. It shrinks routing tables, but it hides detail, so a flapping component can still affect the whole summary.

SVI (Switch Virtual Interface) — A Layer-3 interface that represents a VLAN on a switch, used for management or for routing between VLANs.

Switch — A device that forwards frames within a network using MAC addresses. It learns which MAC is on which port and floods only what it has to.

Syslog — The standard for shipping log messages to a central server. It is the first place to look when something changed at 2 a.m.

T

TACACS+ — A Cisco-originated AAA protocol that separates authentication, authorization, and accounting and encrypts the whole payload. It is common for device administration rather than user access.

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) — A connection-oriented transport that guarantees ordered delivery, retransmits lost data, and adjusts its rate to the network. Web, SSH, and most control traffic use it.

Throughput — The rate actually achieved, as opposed to the link's capacity. Overhead, loss, and latency keep it below the advertised bandwidth.

TLS (Transport Layer Security) — The protocol that encrypts and authenticates application traffic; HTTPS is HTTP inside TLS. It replaced SSL.

Traceroute — A tool that reveals the path by sending packets with increasing TTL values and collecting the "time exceeded" replies. Missing hops usually mean filtering, not a broken path.

Transit — Carrying traffic between two other networks for a fee. It is the opposite of peering.

Trunk — A link that carries several VLANs at once, tagging each frame with its VLAN ID (802.1Q). Access ports carry one untagged VLAN; a trunk is what connects two switches, or a switch to a router that needs to route between VLANs.

TTL (Time to Live) — A counter in the IP header that decreases at every router. At zero the packet is dropped — which stops loops and is what makes traceroute possible.

Tunnel — An encapsulation that makes a packet look like it belongs to another network. VPNs and overlays are built from tunnels.

U

UDP (User Datagram Protocol) — A connectionless transport with no retransmission and no ordering. DNS, DHCP, and voice use it because a late packet is worse than a lost one.

ULA (Unique Local Address) — IPv6 private space, fc00::/7. It is not routable on the internet and plays the role RFC 1918 plays for IPv4.

Unicast — One sender, one receiver, addressed to a single host. It is the normal case for almost all traffic, and it is what a switch forwards using its CAM table instead of flooding.

Underlay — The physical network that carries an overlay's tunnels. If the underlay is unstable, the overlay inherits every problem.

uRPF (Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding) — An anti-spoofing check: accept a packet only if the source address is reachable through the interface it arrived on.

Usable host IP - Any address in a subnet except the network and broadcast addresses. These are the addresses you assign to interfaces, PCs, and gateways; a /28 like 10.0.0.16/28 has usable .17 to .30.

V

Virtualization — Running multiple virtual machines on one physical host through a hypervisor, each with virtual CPUs, memory, disks, and NICs.

VLAN (Virtual LAN) — A logical broadcast domain inside a switch. Ports in different VLANs cannot talk at Layer 2 even when they are on the same physical switch.

VLSM (Variable Length Subnet Mask) — Using different prefix lengths inside one address block so every subnet is sized to its actual need instead of all being equal.

VNI — VXLAN Network Identifier. The 24-bit segment ID inside a VXLAN header, allowing about 16 million segments instead of 802.1Q’s 4094 VLANs.

VPC — Virtual Private Cloud. An isolated virtual network in a public cloud, with its own subnets, route tables, and gateways.

VRF (Virtual Routing and Forwarding) — Several independent routing tables on one device. It lets overlapping addresses coexist, which is the basis of MPLS VPNs and multi-tenant designs.

VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol) — The open-standard first-hop redundancy protocol. It does the job of HSRP without being vendor-specific.

vSwitch — A software switch inside a hypervisor that connects virtual NICs to physical uplinks, usually with VLAN-tagged port groups.

VTEP — VXLAN Tunnel Endpoint. The device that encapsulates and decapsulates VXLAN traffic between the overlay and the underlay.

VXLAN (Virtual Extensible LAN) — A tunnel that carries Layer-2 frames over a Layer-3 network, identified by a 24-bit VNI. It allows far more segments than 802.1Q's 4094 VLANs.

W

WAN (Wide Area Network) — The links that connect sites across a provider's infrastructure, as opposed to the LAN inside one site.

Wildcard mask — The inverse of a subnet mask, used in ACLs and OSPF network statements. A 0 bit means "must match"; a 1 bit means "don't care".

Wireshark — The packet analyzer. It is the only tool that shows what actually crossed the wire, which is why it settles most arguments.

WLC — Wireless LAN Controller. The device that centralises SSIDs, security policy, RF settings, and roaming for lightweight access points.

WPA2 / WPA3 — The current Wi-Fi security standards. WPA2 uses AES-CCMP with a pre-shared key or 802.1X; WPA3 replaces the PSK handshake with SAE and adds protected management frames.

Y

YANG — The data modelling language that describes a device's configuration and state as a structured tree. NETCONF and gNMI both carry YANG-modelled data.

Z

Zero trust — A security model that authenticates and authorizes every request instead of trusting anything because it is "inside". The network becomes transport, not a trust boundary.
